articles.title_orig: As Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize, US takes unprecedented action to cripple the court she served on
articles.title_zh: As Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize, US takes unprecedented action to cripple the court she served on
articles.content_orig:
When South African jurist Navi Pillay won this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, she happened to be at a conference at the Nuremberg Court in Germany, where the landmark trial of Nazi leaders almost 80 years ago laid the foundations for modern international law.
As her colleagues in the human rights community applauded and congratulated the former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge on her win, her first reaction was simply: “Is it true? I thought it must be a joke.”
“If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with (US President Donald) Trump,” she quipped, a reference to how last year’s winner gave her medal to the US president, before adding “it’s very appropriate that I’m with friends, colleagues, all of whom support human rights.”
Hours after Pillay’s win, the Trump administration announced fresh sanctions on the ICC, the body established in 2002 to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
The work of the human rights community and the international legal order have increasingly come under attack in recent years – a fact the Nobel committee was eager to highlight in its decision to recognize Pillay, 85.
By spotlighting Pillay, who has served on several international courts and oversaw a 2025 UN report that concluded that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, the committee said it wanted to “remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace.”
That message was not explicitly directed at any one state. But implicitly, it rebuked those countries – most notably the US – whose actions have weakened international legal institutions.
As part of its efforts to “dismantle” the ICC “brick by brick,” in the words of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the Trump administration on Friday announced sanctions on the ICC itself.
“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” Rubio said in a statement hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was announced.
The measure would cut off the court from US companies and financial services. The US Treasury has issued a six-month waiver for companies to wind down their operations with the court. The State Department said that the six-month window “is intended to provide time” for the court “to demonstrate meaningful progress on diplomatic and legal resolutions that address fundamental US concerns regarding the ICC,” and that it “can be adjusted in response to the success or failure of such efforts to address our concerns.”
The sweeping action faced immediate rebuke from the court and other nations.
The ICC condemned the move as an “assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order,” called on other states to support the court and emphasized that its work would continue.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their “continued and unwavering support” for the court.
“As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the court by the United States,” the statement read.
Several of the court’s prosecutors have already been targeted by US sanctions after it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant in 2024.
Rubio vowed in July to “dismantle” the ICC, accusing it of “waging a war against our country, not with bullets or missiles,” but with “the force of so-called international law.” Neither the US nor Israel are parties to the court, and Washington has challenged its jurisdiction to investigate either country.
The administration’s ire against the ICC goes back to Trump’s first term, when it targeted the court for seeking to investigate alleged war crimes committed by US forces in Afghanistan. The second Trump administration has imposed a slew of sanctions against ICC officials for their attempts to investigate the US and Israel.
Without referencing these efforts, the Nobel committee warned that international law is “an absolute necessity” for peace, even if it has struggled to hold the world’s most powerful actors responsible for their actions.
“History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane,” the committee continued. “The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked.”
Pillay, who has served as a judge at both major international courts and as the UN human rights chief, embodies many of the values the committee wanted to emphasize. She too warned that international law, the ICC in particular and human rights are under attack, undermining the principle that justice is required for lasting peace.
The choice was a brave one, Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CNN. “It is big political actors that are pushing against some of these institutions, against some of the legal orders.”
Choosing an individual, rather than the institutions for which she works, “shows that we as individuals might work towards peace in our different capacities,” Gjerløw added.
Born on September 23, 1941, Pillay grew up in a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, while the country was still under apartheid.
Donations from her local community helped her enroll in classes for non-white students at the University of KwaZulu-Natal and it was there that she first came across transcripts of the Nuremberg Trials. They transfixed her, both by demonstrating the idea of countries coming together to pursue criminal justice and as a framework to understand apartheid-era crimes.
After graduating, she defended anti-apartheid activists, exposed the torture of political detainees and successfully sued to stop her own detained husband from being tortured.
“I won access to lawyers for political prisoners, including Nelson Mandela,” she wrote in a 2021 CNN op-ed . “The first judge’s chambers I entered was my own, in 1995, as the first non-White woman to serve on the High Court.”
However, she never served her full term on South Africa’s High Court as she was elected by the UN General Assembly to be a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which sought to prosecute those responsible for the Rwandan genocide in 1994.
I’ve spent my life fighting for human rights – and the job is not done
Pillay was instrumental in two significant legal precedents set by that tribunal – firstly, that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity and genocide, and secondly, that a defendant could face “charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” the Nobel committee said.
She served as a judge at the ICC from 2003-2008 before being appointed as the UN human rights chief. She is currently a judge at the International Court of Justice in a case where Myanmar has been accused of genocide.
The Nobel committee’s decision to award Pillay the peace prize triggered a backlash from Israel on Friday, which has strenuously denied allegations of genocide.
Netanyahu condemned the Nobel committee, saying it had “lost its moral compass” and accusing Pillay of “lies.”
There has been no reaction yet from Trump, who has made no secret of his desire for the prize.
The Nobel Peace Prize has gone to human rights pioneer Navi Pillay. The South African was integral to the anti-apartheid movement, served as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and recently led the UN commission that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

articles.title_orig: World No. 277 Zhou of China stuns Musetti in Shanghai
articles.title_zh: World No. 277 Zhou of China stuns Musetti in Shanghai
articles.content_orig:
Zhou Yi will never forget this day.
The No. 277 player in the PIF ATP Rankings stunned former World No. 5 Lorenzo Musetti 7-6(7), 3-6, 7-6(1) on Friday evening at the Rolex Shanghai Masters to reach the third round at an ATP Masters 1000 event for the first time.
“It’s been amazing. It’s hard to describe. It’s got to be one of the toughest matches I’ve played,” the 21-year-old from China said. “I really enjoy the process and I’m really happy to still stay on this court the next two days. I’m really happy to see myself play on the centre court again and see myself improve.”
Zhou, a wild card, became the third-lowest-ranked player to reach the third round in Rolex Shanghai Masters history, having won a final-set tie-break in his first-round match against Mattia Bellucci .
The home favourite will next take on Hubert Hurkacz , who ousted Novak Djokovic on Friday. It will be the pair’s first Lexus ATP Head2Head meeting.
Zhou hit 14 aces and saved four of the five break points he faced against Musetti, according to Infosys ATP Stats, to triumph in two hours and 28 minutes.
“I prefer playing aggressive, but I know that the only way the outcome is going to be on my side is for me to play my game,” Zhou said. “I cannot follow what he’s doing. He’s an incredible player, but I need to show him that I’m also capable of standing on the other side of the court.”

articles.title_orig: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.title_zh: Experience: I became the world’s oldest crowd surfer at 99
articles.content_orig:
After retiring at 83, I had a new lease of life creating social media content with my grandson. Then I broke the crowd surfing world record
I n 2013, aged 87, I was playing basketball with my grandson Ross in Ohio while he was home from college. He made a video of me blocking his shot, posted it online, and people really ate it up. We started doing comedy skits together and now have more than 4 million followers on Instagram.
After doing lots of short videos, we decided to make a documentary about my life. As part of it, we compiled my bucket list. One of the things I wanted to do was break a world record. Ross and I spent months thinking of something that would be outrageous, but also fun and inclusive. We settled on me becoming the world’s oldest crowd surfer.
Ross knows the country singer Brantley Gilbert, and he was willing to help us at a show he was playing in Bellville, Texas. Originally, during the crowd surfing, I was going to be strapped to a board Ross had made to protect my back, but it was flexing too much, so he strapped me into a stretcher instead.
I was 99 years and 274 days old the day it happened. It was the first time I’d ever crowd surfed. To break the record, I had to stay up for at least 10 seconds. There were 20,000 people in the crowd – we planned for them to move me in a straight line from the back to the front. But 20 minutes before we were due to start, we saw that everyone in the main crowd was sitting in chairs with gaps between them. Ross started panicking. We used the mosh pit instead, and I travelled in a U-shape from stage right to stage left.
I wore a white T-shirt with a red outline of my face on it so I would stand out from the crowd. Brantley introduced me and said: “I’ll beat you up if you drop Granny.”
I was launched out and I felt as if I was flying. I knew I had to trust everyone. Ross panicked because there was a walkway between both sides of the stage with a 10ft gap and a high fence that I had to be passed over. He jumped the fence as I went across and security people carried me over. I was held up for more than three minutes – nearly an entire song. I was so content. I put my arms out and felt I could touch the sky.
after newsletter promotion
When I got back on the stage, the crowd chanted, “Granny, Granny”. I stood there, soaking it all in. It gave me chills. I was recognised by Guinness World Records for becoming the oldest person to crowd surf at a concert .
Ross comes up with all the ideas. He says he’s Steven Spielberg and I’m Betty White. I only realised how much people liked our videos when I went to the grocery store one day and people were asking to take pictures with me.
This is a whole new life for me. I grew up on a farm in Ohio, the youngest of seven children. We didn’t have TV or a phone. We had chores to do from a young age. During the second world war, I made ammunition in a weapons factory, and I worked in factories until my retirement at 83. I’ve worked hard – it gave me purpose.
The videos are a new kind of work. Meeting people is my favourite part. I’ve met Pope Leo and celebrities like Tom Holland and Bad Bunny on red carpets. I love meeting people who know us from social media. They come up to me and say: “I was lonely and sad in hospital and I watched your videos to lift me up.” People say they’ve reconnected with family after watching Ross and I together. When I’m on my deathbed, I want to know that we made everybody’s day a little better.
I took care of Ross when he was a baby, but this has brought us closer. Before, I only saw him a handful of times a year, but now we live together in Ohio.
I turned 100 this summer, and I had two parties with hundreds of people. I can’t believe I’m 100. I’m the only one out of my siblings who has lived this long. Not all days are peachy. The hardest part of getting older is the aches and pains. Making our videos gives me a purpose, and that boosts me on days I don’t feel so good.
I hope our videos make people realise that it’s never too late to live your best life. If you want to do something new, do it now. Enjoy every moment, because it goes by in the blink of an eye.

articles.title_orig: Amid the challenges of the modern world, Amoris laetitia remains a work in progress
articles.title_zh: Amid the challenges of the modern world, Amoris laetitia remains a work in progress
articles.content_orig:
An Egyptian patriarch, an Indian cardinal, an Australian bishop, a French expert and an Argentine theologian, a married couple from the Philippines. All were present at the first briefing in the Press Office of the Holy See, the varied and universal perspective that Pope Leo XIV wanted to impart to the summit for the ten years of Amoris laetitia .
On the third day of work in the Paul VI Hall, where heads of the Eastern Churches and presidents of Episcopal Conferences, experts and couples sit together with the Pope, some of the participants met with the international media to offer details, ideas, and content that emerged in this event of âlisteningâ and âdialogueâ.
Dialogue, understood as sharing experiences on highly current issues, starting with migration which has separated many families around the world and reshaped everyday life and relationships; then the digital age, which affects the way of building bonds or even simply having dinner; and also accompaniment of new couples after the celebration of the wedding, the formation of priests, helping young people to discover the beauty of married life without âscaringâ them or making them feel under pressure, and closeness to victims of abuse.
In short, the work addressed many themes, many ideas, many experiences already lived or initiatives and proposals in progress. âIt is intense workâ, said Jesuit Father Giacomo Costa, consultant to the General Secretariat of the Synod, who spoke about the methodology adopted in recent days.
That methodology had already been consolidated during the most recent Synods and Consistories, whose sessions were punctuated by conversations, meditations, prayers, testimonies and pastoral experiences on the fruits of Pope Francisâ post-synodal exhortation.
Prayer, in particular is something that âmaybe wonât make the newsâ but is âa fundamental moment to enter the climate of a meeting rooted in prayerâ, Father Giacomo emphasized.
After the âfirst stepsââthat is, the initial forty-eight hours spent âgetting to knowâ, âlistening toâ, and âtrustingâ one another (often for the first time)âwork proceeded in various groups. These groups truly reflected the universality of the Church, with tables comprising participants from China, Poland, Italy, Mexico, Central Asia, and beyond. Each group drafted its own report, which was subsequently shared during the plenary session.
Friday morningâs session provided the âinitial overviewâ, offering a chance to reflect on the âbeauty, challenges, and fragility of families today, and what this asks of our Churchesâ, Costa explained.
The focus was primarily on the changes that have intensified in the decade since the publication of Amoris laetitia . These were not merely ânoveltiesâ but âelements of growing transformationââforemost among them the theme of human mobility, âcited universally by all the groupsâ.
This issue affects âhow we live out family relationshipsâ, touching upon separated couples, grandparents acting as parents to their grandchildren, parenting challenges, difficulties in maintaining bonds or passing on the faith, and interfaith marriages.
All these issues emerged from the stories shared by many of those present in the Paul VI Hall. For instance, Costa noted, âit was emphasized that young people and adults should be prepared to live out their faith in other countries and communities, drawing upon the lessons learned within their familiesâ.
Attention was also drawn to the difficulties faced by many families losing their support networks, as well as the enrichment that new experiences and cultures bring to many households.
The digital revolution of the last decade was also central to âmany stories and experiencesâ. There are also many âcreativeâ initiatives by families who are âorganizing new ways to be togetherâsuch as phone-free dinners for conversation, or methods for staying in touch during migrationâ.
The meeting also addressed the training of seminarians raised in digital culture or coming from âreconstitutedâ families. âHow is their experience incorporated into their formation?â was one of the questions asked. âOne can tangibly sense how fragility becomes a place where God continues to manifest the power of loveâ.
Speaking of fragility, the pastors gathered at the Vatican also acknowledged the fragilities of the Church as a whole.
One of these concerns the âaccompanimentâ of familiesâsomething highly desired and promoted, yet sometimes difficult to implement. âAccompaniment risks becoming a buzzword that unites us in theory but remains to be clarified in practiceâ.
For instance, who actually stays close to couples and their children during crises or in old age? Or, how do we move from marriage preparation to supporting couples throughout their lives to help them live out this vocation?
âAccompaniment is the task of the entire Churchâ, Father Giacomo emphasized; âwe must address it together, from a synodal perspectiveâ.
One point on which everyone agreed was the âpressuresâ many families face today. âAre we, as a Church, adding to them with our own demands?â participants asked.
There was no shortage of accounts regarding the difficulties of the current era: long working hours, violence against women, war, and the issue of âdowriesâ in certain cultures.
âCertain tendencies to idealize can burden families with expectations perceived as unattainable and can scare off young peopleâ. The issue will continue to be discussed in the coming days.
Reflection continues on the highly delicate issue of standing with survivors of abuse and those who have experienced violence. These are people who âneed closeness and their own timeâ, and who must be helped to build âtrustâ in the possibility of experiencing loving relationships and intimacy.
All of this, Father Giacomo Costa emphasized, requires an âextra effortâânamely, taking multiculturalism into account. âShared words can refer to different approachesâ.
The atmosphere is âconstructive, pleasant, and sereneâ; the âapproaches do not conflict, but mutual understanding is needed, as the solutions are not the same. We need a dialogue that allows us to explore different sensibilitiesâ.
Work is therefore underway to ârefine a shared understandingâ and build the kind of âfrank and honest sharingâ called for by the Pope.
The first to take the floor briefly to offer greetings at the press gathering was the Coptic Patriarch of Alexandria, Ibrahim Isaac Sedrak, representing the Catholic Church in Egypt at the Vatican meeting.
He was followed by Cardinal Filipe Neri António Sebastião do Rosario Ferrão, Archbishop of Goa and Daman and President of the Conference of Catholic Bishops of India, who reiterated that âfor us, the family is fundamentalâ. articles.title_orig: How the world fell out of love with French debt
articles.title_zh: How the world fell out of love with French debt
articles.content_orig:
PARIS—Why is France the biggest loser from the ongoing global bond market rout? Combine high indebtedness ( 119 percent of gross domestic product), no parliamentary majority to speak of as everyone positions themselves for a likely presidential runoff, and now student protests, and you have a recipe for institutional investors to dump their holdings of previously prized French debt.
In April 2025, when the introduction of Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs caused an ultimately short-lived “Sell US” trend in the market, eurozone debt was a natural refuge for asset managers. And given the lack of any equivalent to the forty-trillion-dollar US treasury market, investors had to choose from different pools of national debt. There weren’t enough of the best-rated options like Germany and the Netherlands to go around precisely because these governments have run tighter budgets over the years and have less debt on the market. French debt, some have quipped , was the closest you could find to a eurozone safe asset. And so investors continued to pile in, overlooking some already clear facts that should have given them pause.
The first is that Paris struggled to wind down the “whatever it takes” spending sprees it embarked on during the COVID-19 pandemic and the early energy price spike caused by Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Whatever one thinks of the usefulness of the policies at the time, the really alarming fact is that ministries allowed exceptional schemes—ranging from furlough and energy subsidies to bicycle repair vouchers—to go on into 2024 or even to this day.
France’s political class has never been the best at making tough decisions because of the public’s well-known propensity to protest, which has been passed down through the generations. The latest young crop is living up to this French tradition in the current wave of mass protests now rattling the country. Even a swivel-eyed libertarian should sympathize with the more reasonable demands of students, especially for better-equipped schools after a sweltering summer and better salaries to prevent classes going for months without replacement teachers. But more and more of the education budget is instead being swallowed by the Education Ministry’s bulging pensions bill.
The burden of France’s pension system takes up nearly 25 percent of all public spending and is squeezing out spending on the future. Very little can be done because of a second shift that bond markets should have spotted earlier.
The sharp deterioration of France’s political climate started well before the bond market rout. President Emmanuel Macron was reelected by default in May 2022 after a campaign dominated by Russia’s still-new full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The electorate registered their frustration in the subsequent parliamentary elections, where the president’s party and its allies failed to win an absolute majority. This hampered the government’s ability to pass a much-needed pensions reform, which had been postponed two years earlier at the onset of the pandemic. It was ultimately passed using an unpopular constitutional device that allows governments to bypass parliament provided they survive a confidence vote. Voters got their own back in the June 2024 European elections, when Macron’s party did so badly that he decided to call early elections.
This decision was a shock to many but it is true that the then government was clearly not going to be able to pass a budget a few months later. Still, it has left France with a parliament split three ways, between the left, the Macron-compatible centrists, and the far right, which ultimately only came in third. Two centrist governments have come and gone since, barely managing to pass budgets and only at the price of reversing the insufficient pension reform to secure enough left-wing votes.
The third government of the new, balkanized parliament age has been led by the surprisingly resilient Sébastien Lecornu, who resigned after less than twenty-four hours in power last October yet somehow is still prime minister. His government’s strategy is to bring spending back in line with the trajectory to 3 percent, which means a budgetary effort of €54 billion. Exogenous factors like the Strait of Hormuz crisis mean the deficit will still be at 5 percent of GDP next year, but good-faith observers will see that real efforts are being made, especially on the expenditure side. Finally, a taboo is breaking around overprivileged pensioners. Leaving the debate on retirement age to the presidential campaign, the government’s draft 2027 budget instead proposes to no longer fully index pensions above €1,260 a month to inflation, and to lower the ceiling on a special 10 percent tax rebate for pensioners to three thousand euros.
Pensioners vote, so you can imagine how enthusiastic parties that want to win the presidential election are about these measures. Yet the bond market’s recent tank does provide the government with a credible argument that failure to pass the budget will only make the situation worse. Too few left-wing votes are available now, as some of the Socialist Party is open to cooperation with the far-left run by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose reactions to the recent bond market distress have ranged from calling for the European Central Bank to cancel its holdings in French debt to suggesting that the governor of the Banque de France—who has commented on the need for budget discipline in the foreign press—should be tried for treason .
But the far right is trying to build its own credibility on economic affairs, ahead of an expected presidential runoff where its candidate, Marine Le Pen of National Rally, will still need to convince cautious right-wing voters like business owners. When presenting her counterbudget and its unconvincing “ savings plan ” this week, she did keep the door open to whipping her MPs into voting through the government’s budget, provided its flaws were “reversible” once she wins power.
It is easy to despair over the political gridlock and the lack of any obvious debt reduction path. Cynics have taken to saying that only some combination of European Central Bank (ECB) liquidity assistance and an International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout—both coming with stringent conditionality—could work. The situation is bad enough for this suggestion not to be a flippant joke, though ECB representatives have said conditions haven’t deteriorated that far yet. But nor should we just shrug and wait for things to get worse.
The French economy is too big to fail: none of the available European instruments created during the last crisis can afford a France-sized bailout, and the same goes for the IMF. The first step would be to pass a budget that does demand some sacrifices from France’s coddled pensioners. Bonne chance.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation: On sol 1943 of its journey of exploration across the surface of Mars, the Curiosity Rover recorded this selfie at the south rim of Vera Rubin Ridge. Of course a sol is a Martian solar day , about 40 minutes longer than an Earth day. Curiosity's sol 1943 corresponds to Earth date January 23, 2018. Also composed as an interactive 360 degree VR , the mosaicked panorama combines 61 exposures taken by the small car-sized rover's Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). Frames containing the imager's arm have been edited out while the extended background used was taken by the rover's Mastcam on sol 1903. At the top of the rover's mast, sitting above the Mastcam, the laser-firing ChemCam housing blocks out the distant, 5 kilometer high peak of Mount Sharp. On Earth date August 26, 2026, Curiosity marked an total elevation gain of 1 kilometer in its trek from the floor of Gale Crater up the slope of Mount Sharp. articles.title_orig: See sunrise on Mars in breathtaking new NASA images — as mysterious, billion-year-old crags come into view
articles.title_zh: See sunrise on Mars in breathtaking new NASA images — as mysterious, billion-year-old crags come into view
articles.content_orig:
NASA has released stunning images of Mars at dawn, revealing the planet’s mysterious cliffs in unprecedented detail.
The interplanetary photo-op comes courtesy of the space agency’s Curiosity rover, which has been combing the surface of the Red Planet since it was dispatched there in 2012 .
Snapped via the vehicle’s Mastcam on August 11 at 8:30 am Martian time , the photos show a dark blue foreground with distant cliffs illuminated by sunlight — like the interstellar version of an 1800s sublime landscape painting.
“This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona,” said Curiosity project scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, Reuters reported. “You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky.”
This marks the most detailed depiction to date of the yardangs, planetary formations that extend for about 10 miles across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp .
Curiosity has been scaling this 3-mile-high Martian mountain since 2014, notably reaching 0.6 miles in elevation — the most ever ascended on Mars.
As it draws nearer, scientists hope the exploration bot can shed some light on the Yardang layer, which has long baffled researchers.
For one, these anomalous monoliths look quite different from all the terrain the rover has roamed before, according to Vasavada.
Despite forming one billion years ago — roughly the same time as the mountain on which it sits —  this sedimentary patina “doesn’t appear to be part of the continuous stack of layers that make up the layer-cake of Mount Sharp,” the scientist observed.
“It was added on a little later,” Vasavada explained. “It’s above what geologists call an unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top.”
The scientist suspects that the crust was originally wind-blown sediment blown there by volcanic activity.
When this dust hardened into rock, “eons of wind carved ‌up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs,” said Vasavada.
Curiosity is projected to reach the yardangs sometime in 2027-28, whereupon it will use its instruments to sample and analyze the sediment, thereby painting a clearer picture of its provenance.
“That’s what makes it exciting to reach,” Vasavada said in a NASA release . “No one is sure exactly what created this layer.”
Prior studies of Mount Sharp revealed that each layer corresponded to a different geological period, providing insight into the lakes, streams and other water bodies that once covered the surface when Mars was lusher and warmer than the desolate rock it is today.
In 2025, Curiosity dug up some carbon-rich minerals that suggested that the planet’s hostile surface might have even harbored life.
By roving deep into the Yardangs, researchers hope they can get a better sense of the “dawn” of the Red Planet.

articles.title_orig: Tech giants Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys and 5 others lose ability to sponsor African and other foreign workers for US green cards
articles.title_zh: Tech giants Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys and 5 others lose ability to sponsor African and other foreign workers for US green cards
articles.content_orig:
The United States has suspended Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and four other major technology companies from a key employment-based green card programme, affecting skilled foreign workers, including Africans seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship.
The other affected companies are Cognizant, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini, with the US Department of Labor suspending all eight firms from the Permanent Labor Certification programme, commonly known as PERM, amid allegations of misuse and fraud.
PERM is part of the process employers use to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based permanent residency in the United States.
The suspension applies to workers of all nationalities , including African professionals whose green card applications depend on sponsorship from the affected companies.
However, the measure does not stop the companies from recruiting Africans for jobs in Africa or other markets, but restricts their use of the PERM programme to sponsor foreign workers for US permanent residency.
DON'T MISS: 7 US multimillionaire donors gave $189 million to universities in 2026, far more than Africa’s 23 billionaires publicly gave to science and research
The decision comes as the Trump administration increases scrutiny of companies that use foreign labour while cutting jobs in the United States.
Vice President JD Vance singled out Microsoft during a news conference, claiming the company had laid off 6,000 American workers while obtaining 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 permanent residencies.
“Our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said.
“You cannot lay off American workers and replace them with foreign indentured servants,” he added.
Across the US technology sector, more than 131,000 workers have been laid off in 2026, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job cuts in technology companies and start-ups.
Microsoft disputed the administration’s account of its visa use, saying most of its recent filings involved workers already employed in the United States.
“80 percent of the visas were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees,” Microsoft said.
“The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country,” the company added.
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling said the eight companies had requested almost three million foreign workers since 2009, secured more than 230,000 H-1B approvals and obtained more than 100,000 permanent labour certifications.
The Department of Labor also said it had uncovered $22 billion worth of alleged visa fraud.
“Today we are protecting something far more valuable than any dollar amount. We are protecting the American worker,” Sonderling said.
Employment-based immigration has provided a route to US permanent residency for thousands of Africans.
US Office of Homeland Security Statistics data shows that 11,694 African-born people obtained permanent residency through employment-based preference categories in fiscal year 2022, while 89,571 received green cards that year across employment, family, diversity visa and other categories.
In fiscal year 2023, the number of African-born people obtaining permanent residency across all categories rose to 105,520, accounting for about 9% of new permanent residents.
Nigeria accounted for 15,790 of those recipients, although available data does not show how many Africans were sponsored specifically by the eight suspended companies.

articles.title_orig: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.title_zh: BIDMC Researchers Conduct First Real-World Study of Safety and Quality of Patient-Facing AI in Primary Care
articles.content_orig:
BOSTON — The aging population, workforce changes, and patients’ increasingly complex medical needs are all factors straining primary care systems around the world. Artificial intelligence tools have emerged as a potential means of extending the capabilities of health care workers, including in primary care settings. Large language models (LLMs), also known as chatbots, have performed extremely well in simulations. However, little is known about how these systems perform with real patients.
Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) have conducted what they believe is the first prospective real-world study of a patient-facing conversational AI system in primary care, taking an important step toward evaluating the technology through the same kind of rigorous clinical testing used for other health care interventions. The findings appear in The Lancet .
“Despite the theoretical performance of patient-facing AI in experimental settings, it is unclear how conversationally safe these encounters are in a real-world setting," said Adam Rodman, MD, Director of AI Programs at the Carl J. Shapiro Institute for Research and Education at BIDMC. "Before we begin evaluating them as workload interventions, AI tools must first be shown to operate safely and acceptably in real care workflows. With this research, we set out to assess whether this kind of technology could improve both patient and physician experience."
Rodman and colleagues in collaboration with researchers at Google evaluated the Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer (AMIE), a medical AI chatbot that patients used from home after scheduling an urgent primary care appointment with a BIDMC physician. Through a secure text-chat interface, the system asked patients about their symptoms, gathered medical histories, provided possible diagnoses for patients to review with their doctor, and generated a summary for clinician review prior to the visit.
Conducted between April and November 2025, the study enrolled 114 patients, 98 of whom completed both the AI interaction and their primary care appointment. Every conversation was monitored in real time by a board-certified internal medicine physician who could intervene if a patient appeared at risk of harm, experienced significant emotional distress, asked to end the session, or if the physician identified a potential safety concern — such as the need to clarify symptoms, provide emergency care instructions, or address concern about a serious possible diagnosis.
Across all 98 completed encounters, none of the conversations required a safety-stop intervention. Supervising physicians identified one hallucination and provided additional clinical clarification in five cases.
"This study helps establish the baseline characteristics of such real-world conversations,” said co-first author Peter Brodeur, MD, a clinical fellow in cardiovascular medicine at BIDMC. “These baseline characteristics provide a foundation for all future prospective trials aimed at discovering when human-on-the-loop workflows may be appropriate.”
Patients appeared receptive to the technology. Patients rated the quality of AMIE's conversations favorably — as did physician evaluators — across most measures. Moreover, patient attitudes toward AI improved after interacting with the chatbot and remained elevated following their appointment with a clinician.
"One of the most important questions was simply how patients would engage with a conversational AI system in a real clinical setting," said co-first author Jacob Koshy, MD, MPH, a hospitalist in the Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. "By prospectively observing these interactions, we were able to better understand both the opportunities and the limitations of the technology in the context of routine patient care."
While patients gave high marks to the system's ability to listen, explain information, and help them feel at ease, concerns remained around two areas: trust in the confidentiality of information shared with the system and trust in the chatbot's honesty and trustworthiness. Researchers said those findings underscore the importance of continued work to build patient trust as AI tools move into clinical care.
"Research suggests that patient trust in medical AI systems flows from relationships with their human providers," said Rodman. "Future research will need to explore which interaction characteristics can build patient trust and how AI interactions can enhance the patient-physician relationship."
The findings also suggest the technology may have practical value in clinical workflows.
Primary care providers were able to review an AI-generated transcript or summary before seeing their patients for 44 cases. In 75 percent of cases, physicians said doing so helped them prepare for the visit and in 57 percent of cases, they reported it may have influenced their clinical approach. In only one case did a provider report the interaction as somewhat harmful, citing concern that a patient may have experienced anxiety after AMIE included lymphoma among its possible diagnoses.
Rodman and colleagues emphasized that the study was designed to evaluate feasibility rather than to determine whether AI improves health outcomes.
“Our primary care practice — and our hospital — has a long history of rigorously monitoring the safety of the clinical care we provide, and this study serves as an exemplar of how the safety of AI may be assessed prior to clinical implementation,” said co-senior author Marc L. Cohen, MD, Clinical Chief of Primary Care, Division of General Medicine at BIDMC. “We believe the future involves continued involvement of human clinicians in patient care, but see a future where the triad of patient, human clinician, and AI help to provide our patients with the very best evidenced-based care possible," said Cohen.
Co-authors included Ava Homiar, BS; Charles Wu, MD; Hannah M. Ferrera, MD; Lindsey Crowley, MD; Christine G. Kohn, MD; Vinay Kadiyala, MD; Wendy Du, MD; David Feinbloom, MD; Jonathan X. Li, MD; Spencer E. Rittner, MD; and Rob Fields, MD of BIDMC; Selena K. Zhang, BS, of Harvard Medical School; Anil Palepu, PhD; Roma Ruparel, MPH; Joseph Xu, PhD; Amy Wang, MD; Jihyeon Lee, MS; Ellery Wulczyn, MS; Kavita Kulkarni, MS; Jessica M. Williams, BS; Renee Wong, BEcom; Petar Sirkovic, PhD; Alessio Orlandi, PhD; Christopher Semturs, MS; Yun Liu, PhD; Juraj Gottweis, MS; Dale R. Webster, PhD; Katherine Chou, MS; Avinatan Hassidim, PhD; Yossi Matias, PhD; James Manyika, DPhil; and Mike Schaekermann, PhD, of Google Research; and Khaled Saab, PhD; Ryutaro Tanno, PhD; David Stutz, PhD; Wei-Hung Weng, MD; David Barrett, PhD; Elahe Vedadi, PhD; S. Sara Mahdavi, PhD; Tao Tu, PhD; Joëlle Barral, PhD; Pushmeet Kohli, PhD; Vivek Natarajan, MS; and Alan Karthikesalingam, PhD, of Google DeepMind.
This study was funded by Alphabet. Adam Rodman, MD, served as a visiting researcher at Google during part of the study. Full disclosures are available in the published manuscript.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center is a leading academic medical center, where extraordinary care is supported by high-quality education and research. BIDMC is a teaching affiliate of Harvard Medical School, and consistently ranks as a national leader among independent hospitals in National Institutes of Health funding. BIDMC is the official hospital of the Boston Red Sox.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center is a part of Beth Israel Lahey Health , a healthcare system that brings together academic medical centers and teaching hospitals, community and specialty hospitals, more than 4,700 physicians and 39,000 employees in a shared mission to expand access to great care and advance the science and practice of medicine through groundbreaking research and education.

articles.title_orig: Wall St climbs as oil slips; SpaceX spectrum deal weighs on telecoms
articles.title_zh: Wall St climbs as oil slips; SpaceX spectrum deal weighs on telecoms
articles.content_orig:
Telecommunications stocks sold off on Friday after Elon Musk 's SpaceX announced an agreement to purchase a nationwide spectrum portfolio , aiming to expand its Starlink internet into mobile service.
Verizon was down roughly 7% on the news, and is pacing its worst day since 2002. Shares of T-Mobile were down 12% while AT&T fell around 10%. SpaceX stock climbed slightly, around 1% for the day.
The deal includes acquiring the spectrum from Grain Management, which SpaceX described as a "license portfolio of up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band," in a Thursday statement.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whose agency will oversee approval of the deal, said that competition in the spectrum market was "really good news for the American consumers" in a CNBC interview.
"We're probably going to bring over $100 billion of spectrum into the market over the next two years, so we're seeing a lot of competition," Carr told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday.
"There's going to be moves in the market. People are going to try to out-compete, out-innovate, and I think that's great. We're going to see how this plays out. It's not for us ultimately to pick winners and losers," he added.

articles.title_orig: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life
articles.title_zh: End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland review – Murakami’s marvel brilliantly brought to life
articles.content_orig:
Barbican theatre, London With a dual narrative set in Tokyo and a world of dreams, Philippe Decouflé’s epic production is as bewitching as its balletic unicorns
H ow to stage Haruki Murakami’s epic, dual-narrative novel without leaving the audience in a muddle? Director-choreographer Philippe Decouflé goes big, filling the enormous Barbican stage with a kaleidoscope of dream worlds for Ako Takahashi’s adaptation. It could have become a scramble of stories and inquiries into memory, technological advances in society and the imagination. Instead, it is turned into one long immaculate coup de théâtre.
There are two versions of the protagonist, Watashi (Tatsuya Fujiwara) – one is in Tokyo, the other in a world comprising dreams. The city is noirish while the latter is beautiful but dangerous, with a complicated storyline involving the sundering of humans from their shadows, a walled city, roaming animals and a professor (Narushi Ikeda) who collects their skulls to channel past experiences through sound.
The professor’s 17-year-old granddaughter (Miu Tomita) accompanies Watashi in Tokyo and appears like a kitsch version of the prophetess who goes with Aeneas into the underworld. Watashi seeks escape, so he can be reunited with his shadow (Shuntaro Miyao), but is drawn to this strange world too and has a romance with a librarian (Misato Morita).
Initially, it spirals into a rabbit hole of wonderlands, with kooky humour and references to western canonical and pop culture, as is Murakami’s way, from ancient myth to Lewis Carroll’s Alice and Luis Buñuel’s Un Chien Andalou. A playful set, designed by K Ishihara, shows its own theatrical construction with cheeky playfulness.
The visual pyrotechnics suck you in, from big projections to the speed, flow and agility of dancing that gestures at anime. They bring forth Murakami’s many creatures, from underground “murks”, with porcupine spikes, who flip and cartwheel, to a herd of balletic unicorns.
Decouflé’s choreography is unsurpassable in its elastic grace and athleticism without seeming circus-like. The aesthetics on the whole are so ravishing that it doesn’t matter if the story is not easy to grasp in the first half. At least not for some because, while Murakami fans will know that the unity of the story is to come, initiates to his work may be left punch-drunk and befuddled by the onslaught of worlds and images.
It becomes clear after the interval that this is controlled and deliberate confusion, reflecting Watashi’s state of mind. The dance becomes imbued with feeling as Murakami’s world reveals its underlying themes of loneliness, grief, the fear of disappearing and of death.
But the story of lost shadows, representing the “true” self, bears bigger socio-political echoes that feel contemporary, and even prescient (the book was published in 1985). This world looks like Neo’s in The Matrix, and its technology chimes with ideas in Naomi Klein’s book, Doppelganger: A Trip into the Mirror World . The sinister side of the perfectionism that this dream society has cultivated could be a comment on postwar Japan, or on our world of AI, real and fake selves, code and machine-constructed subjectivity.
At almost three hours, it leaves you with the sense that you have been dreaming, collectively, about a world of dead animals, lost shadows and unfeeling humans, but also of unicorns, impossible beauty and an ocean-like imagination. It is both of our world, and other.

articles.title_orig: As World Health Summit opens, IRC warns global health investment in fragile states is declining as disease outbreaks pose growing threat
articles.title_zh: As World Health Summit opens, IRC warns global health investment in fragile states is declining as disease outbreaks pose growing threat
articles.content_orig:
More than 70% of epidemic-prone diseases now occur in fragile and conflict-affected countries, where weak health systems allow diseases like Ebola to spread undetected and cross borders, as global health funding collapses to 15-year low.
Progress is possible: the IRC and partners have delivered over 40 million vaccine doses to underimmunized children in crisis settings.
The IRC urges decisionmakers gathered at the World Health Summit to restore health funding to crisis settings, release pledged Ebola funds and partner with humanitarian organizations to reach communities beyond the reach of traditional health systems.
Berlin, Germany, October 9, 2026 — As global health leaders gather in Berlin for the World Health Summit, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) warns that a sharp retreat in global health spending is putting lives and hard-won health gains at risk in the world’s most fragile and conflict-affected states.
The consequences of that retreat are increasingly urgent. In eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), an outbreak of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola–for which there is no approved vaccine– has spread across seven provinces and into neighboring Uganda and Kenya. Since the first case was confirmed in May, nearly 8,500 people have been infected and more than 4,000 have died.
“Every dollar cut from health in fragile states is a risk to lives and livelihoods not just locally but globally,” said Alyoscia D’Onofrio, vice president and head of technical excellence at the IRC. “Resilience is built in the places where crises begin. We have shown that it’s possible to cost-effectively vaccinate children even in the most hard–to-reach places if we have the resources.”
IRC has proven progress in fragile and conflict-affected states is possible. The Gavi-funded Reaching Every Child in Humanitarian settings (REACH) consortium, led by the IRC, has now delivered more than 40 million vaccine doses to children in six conflict-affected countries, up from 20 million a year ago . REACH was built for communities that government health systems cannot safely reach, some of which had not seen a vaccine in more than a decade. When it launched in 2022, humanitarian organizations could access just 16% of its 156 target communities; today they reach all of them.
Those hard-won gains are now at risk as donors cut health budgets to a 15-year low - widening the gulf in health equity and outcomes between fragile and stable settings. In Afghanistan alone, the number of health facilities the IRC supports fell by 70% in 2025. Fragile and conflict-affected settings experience more than 70% of global outbreaks of epidemic-prone diseases such as cholera, measles and meningitis. One in five of the world’s children now live in these countries, where children face a mortality rate three times higher than their peers in stable settings, and are three times less likely to receive any routine vaccines. The maternal mortality ratio for a woman living in a fragile or conflict-affected setting is five times higher than her peers in stable settings.
The IRC is calling on governments, donors and multilateral institutions at the World Health Summit to:
The IRC is a global leader in delivering essential health services and building resilient health systems in fragile and conflict-affected areas. The IRC's health programs are designed to address both immediate crises and long-term challenges faced by vulnerable populations worldwide, focusing on foundational primary health care programming – ensuring we continue to deliver lifesaving services during crisis and recovery, while building resilient health systems. In FY2025, the International Rescue Committee (IRC) delivered vital health services to nearly 17 million people.
The International Rescue Committee responds to the world’s worst humanitarian crises, helping to restore health, safety, education, economic wellbeing, and power to people devastated by conflict and disaster. Founded in 1933 at the call of Albert Einstein, the IRC works in more than 40 countries and in 30 U.S. cities helping people to survive, reclaim control of their future, and strengthen their communities. Learn more at www.rescue.org and follow the IRC on Instagram , Facebook , TikTok , LinkedIn and Bluesky .

articles.title_orig: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
articles.title_zh: Two men deny Iran-backed surveillance of Jewish and Israeli sites in London
articles.content_orig:
Two men have pleaded not guilty to carrying out surveillance on Jewish and Israeli sites across London on behalf of Iran's intelligence service.
Nematollah Shahsavani, 41, and Alireza Farasati, 22, are accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service under the National Security Act 2023.
Prosecutors allege the pair carried out hostile reconnaissance at several locations between 9 July and 15 August last year.
Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue.
Both defendants entered their not not guilty pleas during an appearance at the Old Bailey on Friday. Farasati appeared in person in the dock, while Shahsavani attended via video link from HMP Pentonville.
The court previously heard that police confiscated electronic devices from Farasati, a barber, when he was stopped on 14 August last year.
Prosecutors allege that Shahsavani directed Farasati to monitor and gather intelligence on London's Jewish and Israeli communities. Shahsavani, who works as a car salesman and delivery driver, was allegedly acting on instructions from Iranian intelligence.
Shahsavani, a dual British-Iranian national and father of two from North Finchley, north London, has lived in the UK since 2009.
Farasati, an Iranian national living in Colindale, north-west London, arrived in Britain as a 17-year-old in 2021.
Mrs Judge Cheema-Grubb scheduled a further pre-trial hearing for 12 February, with a full trial due to begin at the Old Bailey on 26 April next year.
Both men, who were detained in March, remain in custody.

articles.title_orig: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
articles.title_zh: ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting
articles.content_orig:
Immigration officer shot man in car where five-year-old child was sitting, sparking fierce protests
Leading New York Democrats expressed anger and demanded curbs on Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) violence after a federal officer shot a man driving a car in which his five-year-old son was sitting, sparking fierce protests .
At least seven shots were reportedly fired and the man was hit in the neck late on Thursday afternoon as children were coming home from school in the busy Marble Hill neighborhood of New York City. Marble Hill considered part of Manhattan, but is physically located in the Bronx.
Federal authorities on Friday morning identified Oscar Belgal as the man shot, saying he was undocumented, from the Dominican Republic and had a felony record and gang affiliations.
Marcos Charles, a senior ‌ICE official, said Belgal refused ​to exit his car when approached by ‌federal officers who were trying to arrest him, and then accelerated, ‌struck two ICE vehicles and drove towards other officers. An ICE officer then shot Belgal and Charles said the wound was “superficial”.
Footage showed a man in a high-visibility construction vest, possibly with a badge on a lanyard, carrying an assault-style rifle and standing close to Belgal, who is sat on the street, while another officer appears to hold a hand to his neck and shoulder area.
New York police officers in uniform shortly afterwards carry the man to an unmarked car and lay him in the back seat, handcuffed behind his back.
But Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York congresswoman, and Zohran Mamdani , the city’s mayor – all of whom are Democrats – led strong condemnation of ICE’s conduct.
Darializa Avila Chevalier, the Democratic New York candidate, rushed to the protests and was knocked over in the chaos as local police and demonstrators clashed.
The wounded man was conscious and hospitalized, authorities said .
A joint statement from Manhattan and Bronx borough presidents Vanessa L Gibson and Brad Holyman-Sigal, respectively, said the man then was “reportedly transferred to a detention facility out of New York state”.
“Today, the Bronx and Manhattan stand united in outrage” over the case, Gibson and Holyman-Sigal’s statement said. “The frustration, pain, anger and trauma stoked by this incident extends far beyond an individual.”
Mamdani called the incident “unconscionable” and said on Thursday night that ICE, part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), had “whisked him away” from the New York-Presbyterian Allen hospital in upper Manhattan.
A similar incident occurred in Texas last month after a man was shot by an ICE officer in Austin and despite a bullet lodged in his back was taken by the federal authorities from a local hospital to ICE detention about 140 miles away.
Ocasio-Cortez and Mamdani demanded ICE be abolished.
Both Hochul and Mamdani spoke to Donald Trump and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, by phone on Thursday night.
“I have been on ​the phone with President Trump and Secretary Mullin negotiating ‌the release of the man ICE agents ‌shot. Those negotiations were unsuccessful,” Mamdani told a press conference. He demanded from the Trump ‌administration that ICE stop its enforcement actions in New York City. “ICE is rotten to its core,” he said.
ICE has been stepping up arrests all year despite withdrawing massed militarized ranks from Minneapolis in January and adopting a more covert approach to enforcement .
Both Hochul and Mamdani demanded that ICE cease enforcement operations in New York and the governor said she expressed outrage to the Trump administration on behalf of all New Yorkers. Hochul added that the incident could easily have ended in tragedy.
“No child should ever have to experience the terror of gunfire,” she said. The child was being looked after by his family on Friday.
The streets where the shooting and protests took place were calm on Friday morning but many residents remained shocked and angry.
“Here’s an innocent child that was caught in the crossfire,” said Calvin Hayden, a south Bronx native. “That child could have been killed.” Hayden heard about the shooting the night before and said he was immediately disturbed. He came to Marble Hill, the northernmost part of Manhattan, to see the aftermath.
“I don’t believe ICE has any reason or right to be in New York City,” he said, adding he thought New York was already equipped on its own to handle immigration disputes without ICE presence.
“There’s a lot of individuals who are not committing crimes and they just want to make a better life for themselves,” he said.
Some drivers on 225th Street yelled anti-ICE sentiments as they drove past the scene.
Mullin said on Friday morning that the ICE officers involved in the shooting did not know there was a child in the vehicle and defended the agency’s actions. But he pointed out that Belgal would have obviously known the child was in his car when he drove it at officers. The exact sequence of events leading up to the shooting have not yet become clear.
Mullin said that Hochul had asked the DHS for a pause on enforcement in New York.
“No, we are not putting a pause on enforcement,” he said.
Mullin criticized New York’s “sanctuary” policies , ​which restrict how much city agencies and police cooperate with immigration authoritie.
Belgal, 28, has prior convictions, was serving five years of probation for felony grand larceny and was also arrested on drug charges in 2025, a case that is still pending, according to the New York police department.
“What happened today was an outrage,” Mamdani said late on Thursday, adding: “When ICE agents opened fire, a five-year-old child – a five-year-old child! – was in the back seat of that car. Thank God that child is physically unharmed.”
Witnesses told local media they heard the child yelling at the officers after the shooting. At least 20 people have been shot by federal immigration agents under the second Trump administration, as well as a rise in deaths in detention.
“ICE is a rogue, lawless and paramilitary surveillance agency. It does not belong in New York City and it should not exist in the United States of America. Abolish ICE,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement.
The representative also condemned the retail company Target for allowing federal enforcement teams to use its parking lots as staging areas from which to launch arrest operations.
Protesters held signs saying:“Jail all killer ICE agents” and “Leave our neighbors alone.”
“ICE, get the fuck out of our neighborhood,” shouted Gibson, the Bronx borough president. “I’m angry that we have to be here … We are a working-class community. We don’t deserve this type of treatment from the White House.” She encouraged the crowd to get involved in opposing ICE, saying: “There are more of us than there are of them. I want this to be a moment that we turn into a movement.”
Protesters gathered at the hospital where Belgal was taken. The police set up barricades and protesters quickly clashed with officers in a chaotic scene.
Demonstrators banged drums and shouted: “Shut it down,” and “ICE out!” as cars driving by honked in support.
Standing outside the hospital, Murad Awawdeh, the president of the New York Immigration Coalition, said he wanted to see an independent investigation into the shooting led by New York officials.
“The pain that you’re witnessing is people who are witnessing their neighbors, their family members, their friends being ripped away,” he said.
ICE has arrested more than 19,500 people in New York and nearly 18,000 in New Jersey during the second Trump administration, mostly Latin American immigrant men without criminal histories, Gothamist reported earlier this week using government data, adding that those totals were more than double the number of such arrests in the last 18 months of the Biden administration.
Lex McMenamin and Joanna Walters contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Calidore String Quartet Performs World Premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens
articles.title_zh: Calidore String Quartet Performs World Premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens
articles.content_orig:
The Calidore String Quartet will give the world premiere of Anna Clyne’s The Seven Ravens at Konserthuset Stockholm on 10 October . Co-commissioned by Konserthuset Stockholm, Shriver Hall Concert Series and The Phillips Collection, the work will also feature on a forthcoming album of Clyne’s complete chamber works, to be released on Signum Records. The Stockholm programme pairs Clyne’s new work with Dvořák’s String Quartet No. 12, “The American” , and Korngold’s String Quartet No. 3.
The quartet will give the US premiere of The Seven Ravens at Baltimore’s Shriver Hall in May 2027 . The programme will also include Haydn’s String Quartet in D major, Caroline Shaw’s Entr’acte and Beethoven’s String Quartet in B-flat major.
Elsewhere in the 2026/27 season, the Calidore String Quartet will tour extensively across North America, with engagements at New York’s Lincoln Center and in Montreal and Portland, a tour of California, and a Beethoven residency in Denver. In Europe, the quartet returns to Amsterdam, London’s Wigmore Hall and Padova.

articles.title_orig: SPCX Stock Surges Premarket – JPMorgan Says SpaceX May Need Ground-Based Network To Rival Telecom Giants
articles.title_zh: SPCX Stock Surges Premarket – JPMorgan Says SpaceX May Need Ground-Based Network To Rival Telecom Giants
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
JPMorgan said SpaceX would likely need to deploy a terrestrial network using large cell towers.
KeyBanc called SpaceX's spectrum acquisition a positive for tower operators.
Despite the dip in share prices, JPMorgan sees limited near-term competitive risk for U.S. wireless carriers.
SpaceX (SPCX) could need to build a ground-based mobile network to compete with established U.S. telecom operators following its latest spectrum acquisition, JPMorgan said on Friday.
The firm maintained its 'Overweight' rating on SpaceX, saying the agreement makes Starlink Mobile's long-term opportunity more credible, although building a competitive network would require significant investment, according to TheFly.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
The stock was up 3.7% in pre-market trading, while SPCX was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing.
On Thursday, SpaceX announced an agreement to acquire Grain Management's nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum licenses, covering up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum. Grain confirmed that SpaceX would acquire its entire portfolio, subject to Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approval.
SpaceX said that the frequencies address an important technical gap in Starlink Mobile's push to become a major mobile carrier.
The acquisition follows SpaceX's earlier purchase of higher-frequency spectrum from EchoStar and supports its ambition to combine satellite connectivity with traditional mobile infrastructure.
JPMorgan said SpaceX would likely need to deploy a terrestrial network using large cell towers unless it secures a mobile virtual network operator agreement, which would allow it to use an existing carrier's network.
This brings tower operators into play. KeyBanc analyst Brandon Nispel called the acquisition positive for tower operators, saying SpaceX's strategy appears to be shifting toward traditional cell towers rather than smaller cellular equipment. The firm also suggested SpaceX could potentially take over some existing DISH Network tower leases.
Goldman Sachs echoed the sentiment, saying it expects SpaceX to deploy the 800 MHz spectrum via cell towers in major cities and other urban areas to strengthen its mobile network coverage.
Tower operators surged in pre-market trading on Friday. American Tower (AMT), Crown Castle (CCI) and SBA Communications (SBAC) were up around 8% each.
Meanwhile, shares of AT&T (T), Verizon (VZ) and T-Mobile (TMUS) fell between 5% and 7%, over competition and a potential long-term disruption of the industry. However, JPMorgan sees limited near-term competitive risk for U.S. wireless carriers.
Retail sentiment surrounding SPCX trended in the 'Bullish' zone on Stocktwits over the past 24 hours, amid 'high' message volumes.
One user said the spectrum deal is going to generate a lot of revenue for SpaceX.
However, another user highlighted market risks.
SPCX shares have gained around 23% from their IPO price.

articles.title_orig: IonQ Achieves Record 1 kHz Quantum Interconnect Speed
articles.title_zh: IonQ Achieves Record 1 kHz Quantum Interconnect Speed
articles.content_orig:
COLLEGE PARK, Md. – Oct. 9, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced the achievement of entanglement rates above 1,000 per second (1 kHz) between a trapped ion qubit and a solid-state memory, through a photonic interconnect. Entanglement is the quantum connection that lets separate systems work together, and it is the essential ingredient for networking quantum computers. While the trapped ion qubit sets the standard for qubit coherence, the solid-state quantum memory has unmatched efficiency coupling to light. Their juxtaposition is the best of both worlds, demonstrating the fastest quantum interconnect rate between qubits of any platform.
“IonQ has crossed a pivotal milestone for memory enhanced quantum interconnects, achieving more than 1,000 entanglement events per second,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ. “Classical data centers achieved massive scale by connecting specialized processors, memory, and networks. Quantum systems will scale in much the same way. This breakthrough addresses a critical interconnect bottleneck and advances IonQ’s roadmap to build the networked quantum data centers of the future.”
A technical paper presents results from real-world hardware testing of an end-to-end link between a trapped ion system and a silicon vacancy (SiV) qubit, building on IonQ’s SiV quantum memory platform . IonQ’s demonstration achieves rates more than four times faster than the previous record 1 for trapped ions, held by IonQ co-founder Chris Monroe’s research group at Duke University, also a collaborator on the paper.
“IonQ’s efforts in quantum interconnects go back over a decade, to the founding of the company. Moving qubits through photons will be necessary in any large-scale quantum computer, and this demonstration sets the foundation for some amazing work to come,” said Monroe, Chief Scientist at IonQ and Gilhuly Family Presidential Distinguished Professor at Duke University.
“This work shows that a photonic quantum interconnect need not be a bottleneck for distributed quantum computing,” said Mihir Bhaskar, IonQ SVP and GM of Quantum Technologies at SkyWater. “Our technology can interface with almost any qubit type, so we see this unlocking a wide range of opportunities across multiple hardware modalities, from modular computing to networked sensing and beyond.”
This quantum memory and interconnect approach is also driving IonQ’s work with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s ( DARPA) HARQ program , which seeks to develop high-speed quantum interconnects compatible with multiple computing qubit types. While this latest demonstration used trapped ion systems, the underlying architecture is expected to be compatible with multiple qubit approaches. This may include neutral atoms and superconducting systems with transducers (devices that convert microwave signals into light).
IonQ’s memory and interconnect platform is likewise ramping up commercially, with the first commercial sale to the University of Maryland announced in April, and a second system sale to SDT in South Korea, announced in September.
Additional technical details can be found in the arXiv preprint.
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: What Microsoft’s green card suspension means for Seattle-area workers
articles.title_zh: What Microsoft’s green card suspension means for Seattle-area workers
articles.content_orig:
India called comments by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance about immigrants from the country "deeply offensive" in an official government statement published on Friday.
Vance said on Thursday that the Trump administration wants foreign and local companies to "employ American workers," and that they "cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants."
He was speaking as the U.S. Department of Labor announced it would suspend Microsoft , Adobe and several major Indian information technology companies from its Permanent Labor Certification program, meaning they cannot apply for permanent residency for their employees on H-1 B visas.
Around 70% of H-1B beneficiaries in 2025 were born in India , per official data .
In a statement on Friday, India's Ministry of External Affairs accused Vance of using " terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations."
"Such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem," the statement said.
Vance's office did not immediately respond to a comment request from CNBC.
Vance was critical of Microsoft, accusing the company of replacing 6,000 laid-off workers with people on H-1B visas.
The Indian foreign ministry assured its citizens that measures announced by the U.S. will not affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents.
"Talent mobility adds value to both economies," the statement said, adding that the suspensions "do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries."
The Indian companies affected by the ban include Cognizant , Infosys , Capgemini, Tata Consultancy Services , Wipro and HCL .
NASSCOM, the IT industry body, said in a statement that Indian technology companies have "significantly reduced their dependence on H-1B visas" over the last few years, and are expanding domestic hiring to their U.S. workforces.
The largest Indian IT company, Tata Consultancy Services, said its H-1B applications were in "single digits" in the last two years, and it intends to hire another 15,000 people in the U.S. over the next five years.
In June, a federal judge blocked the $100,000 H-1B visa fee U.S. President Donald Trump imposed last year.

articles.content_orig:
Subscribe today from as little as £2 / $2.70 a month! Find out more
Subscribe from £2 / $2.70 a month! Find out more
Occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island have fallen by 63% since 2011, scientists say, with warming seas pushing the penguins' krill prey out of reach
The world’s largest penguin colony has lost its title after a steep decline in chinstrap penguins on a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, according to new research by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
The study, published in the journal Current Biology, found that the number of occupied chinstrap nests on Zavodovski Island, in the South Sandwich Islands, fell by 63% between 2011 and 2025. The island now has the highest rate of chinstrap decline anywhere in the world, and the title of largest colony passes to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea, more than 5,000km away.
In 2011, Zavodovski was home to an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said Prof Norman Ratcliffe, the BAS penguin ecologist who led the research.
The researchers say the cause is climate-driven change in the Southern Ocean. Chinstraps have a specialist diet and prefer cooler water, and tracking data showed they forage to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill. As the water warms, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
“Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food,” Ratcliffe said.
The island’s macaroni penguins, which have a broader diet and can switch to fish and crustaceans when krill become scarce, increased by 28% between 2011 and 2016 and have been stable since. Tracking data showed them foraging in warmer waters to the north-east. Ratcliffe described the shift as the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica.
Scientists again advise zero cod catch across UK waters to prevent stock collapse
Water companies failed to report more than 50,000 sewage discharges on time, campaigners say
Restored oyster reefs could be worth $12 trillion a year, study finds
Warming seas are reshuffling plankton and the marine food web
Seagrass bounces back in Cairns, but fish populations are changed
The team travelled for 15 days by yacht to reach the island, which is more than 2,000km from the nearest permanent human settlement. They used drone surveys, aerial photography from an RAF aircraft based in the Falklands, and tracking devices fitted to penguins.
The scientists ruled out several other explanations. Zavodovski’s volcano, Mount Curry, erupted in March 2016, but the decline began years earlier and has been steady, and the researchers say it is not to blame. They also dismissed competition between the two penguin species for nesting space, and krill fishing, because harvesting is banned in the marine protected area surrounding the island. However, it is unclear how krill fishing in areas connected by currents to the protected area might be affecting wider food supplies.
The South Sandwich Islands hold around 30% of the world’s chinstrap population. The researchers say the declines here, together with those elsewhere in Antarctica, could tip the species into the “Endangered” category on the IUCN Red List.
Ratcliffe warned that the loss of chinstraps could have wider consequences for marine food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely,” he told the Guardian.
Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specialises in remote sensing of penguins, said the findings showed that even the most remote places were affected by climate change. “Not even they can escape the impacts of climate change,” he said.
The study comes six months after emperor penguins were declared an endangered species because of sea ice loss.
