articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as tech shares rebound following sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as tech shares rebound following sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. stock futures edged higher Friday, led by tech, following a losing session in which an underwhelming revenue report from OpenAI took some steam out of the high-flying artificial intelligence trade.
Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.8%. S&P 500 futures climbed 0.4%, while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures advanced 82 points, or 0.2%.
The State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) traded 1% higher. Tech shares broadly were led by a 4% gain in SpaceX. The Elon Musk-led space and satellite company rose on a deal to buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio. Shares of AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile slid as investors wondered worried the agreement could drive up competition.
Other tech names that advanced on Friday include Lumentum and KLA , which gained 5% and 2%, respectively.
AI stocks dropped on Thursday after CNBC confirmed that OpenAI told investors that it saw $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September. Last month, a $68 billion figure was widely reported, though a person familiar with the matter said it also included gross revenue from partners.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 1%, marking its biggest one-day loss since mid-August. Thursday marked the second down day in a row for the tech-heavy index after it climbed to fresh all-time records earlier in the week.
"The sell-off reflected extreme positioning imbalances that have further to unwind in our view, which is why the whole AI-linked tech stock complex is unlikely to simply stage a sharp, V-shaped rebound," wrote Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge.
"When it comes to AI, the main issue isn't the gross vs. net issue with [annualized recurring revenue] but instead: 1) the fact that the standalone frontier labs are increasingly unattractive businesses ... and 2) growing signs that markets are pushing back on the tidal wave of AI-linked debt and equity being thrown at them," he added.
The Dow and Nasdaq Composite are both around flat week to date. The broad S&P 500 is on track for a gain of 0.6% for the week.
Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket:
Shares of Delta Air Lines fell 4% after the company reported its first earnings miss in two years and cut its 2026 outlook .
Third-quarter earnings per share came in at $1.72, adjusted, while revenue totaled $17.59 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $1.75 per share on revenue of $17.67 billion.
For 2026, the airline sees adjusted earnings per share in a range of $5.10 to $5.60. In July, that outlook sat in a range of $6.50 to $7.50. The company pointed to higher fuel prices for the guidance downgrade.
Apple shares were seen around 2% lower in premarket, after Nikkei Asia reported that the company has told some suppliers to cut production of components for its new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models. CNBC has reached out to Apple for comment.
Telecoms stocks including AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile were all sharply lower following a SpaceX deal that will boost its drive to become a mobile carrier competitor in the U.S. SpaceX shares were up nearly 4% early Friday.
Humana meanwhile popped 14% after the insurer was upgraded in closely watched Medicare Advantage quality ratings data.
Treasury yields steadied early Friday as traders assessed President Donald Trump's pledge to not attack Iran until after the midterm elections.
Yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — were holding firm at 5.2399%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also unchanged at 5.6139%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was more than 2 basis points higher at 4.7827%.
European stocks popped in early Friday trade, with the regional Stoxx 600 index up 0.8% at 8:18 a.m. in London and many sectors trading more than 1% higher.
Mining stocks led the charge, up 1.8%, amid concerns of a copper supply squeeze due to strikes at several major operations. Retailers were also 1.6% higher.
Telecommunication stocks tumbled more than 2%, with Deutsche Telecom down 7%, after a SpaceX deal that will give the company greater reach in the U.S. telecoms market rattled U.S. incumbent players AT&T , Verizon and T-Mobile in extended trading. Deutsche Telecom is the parent company of T-Mobile US.
Airtel Money, the mobile banking unit of London-listed telecoms group Airtel Africa , is set to begin conditional trading of its shares on Friday ahead of its admission to the London Stock Exchange on Oct. 14.
The company has set 270 million shares at a fixed price of £1.96 ($2.60), implying an estimated market capitalization at admission of £5.3 billion.
Airtel Money reported $1.35 billion in revenue and $676 million in adjusted earnings in the year to June 2026 and has 53 million monthly active users.
The float is expected to be one of the biggest in the U.K. capital since fintech Wise made its £8.75 billion IPO in 2021. Wise has since moved its main listing to New York in a major blow to London, which has lost a steady stream of mid- to large-scale companies in recent years.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said in a September note that investors would be "rejoicing as the UK stock market is finally getting an IPO that isn't a tiny natural resources company," but noted that Airtel Money would not raise new money from the sale, which will come from existing minority shareholders including TPG and the Qatar Investment Authority,
Asia-Pacific markets closed mostly higher Friday.
Mainland China's CSI 300 advanced 0.16% to 4,317.26, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.4% in its last hour of trade.
Japan's Nikkei 225 was little changed at 69,030.92, while the Topix rose 0.33% to 4,104.81.Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.64% to 8,716.6.
South Korean markets were closed for a holiday.
U.S. Treasury yields were largely stable on Friday, with the benchmark 10-year yield falling less than one basis point to 5.227%, while the 30-year yield was little changed at 5.608%.
Both remained near multi-decade highs amid concerns over persistent inflation and elevated government borrowing.
Swiss private bank UBP raised its estimated fair-value range for the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.75%–5.25% in its October outlook, citing renewed inflationary pressures. The bank said in a note on Friday that risks to yields had become more balanced, although visibility remained limited, prompting it to maintain a neutral duration stance of four years and favor income from bond holdings rather than taking directional bets on interest rates.
UBP also expects the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy gradually, with rate cuts unlikely before the second half of 2027.
Oil fell Friday as U.S. President Donald Trump's comments on Iran calmed nerves, following reports that America was considering resuming strikes against Tehran.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 0.77% to $103.48 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November declined 0.68% to $90.87 per barrel.
Trump said in a post on Truth Social the U.S. "will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," and was having "productive discussions" with Iran.
"In the meantime, accelerated IEA-coordinated stock releases and greater use of alternative export routes could help limit supply pressures," said Thadeu Dos Santos, regional director at markets trading platform Infinox.
"Saudi Arabia's continued use of its restored East-West pipeline is also allowing more crude to reach international markets without relying on the Strait of Hormuz, providing some offset to the upside risks," he added.
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.

articles.title_orig: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
articles.title_zh: Antarctica’s penguins are sending us a distress signal
articles.content_orig:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.
We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?
Something is breaking in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
This story was originally published by The Guardian and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed. Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, professor Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian reported in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem. The new study, published on Wednesday in the journal Current Biology , indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird — which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek — may need to be classified as an endangered species.
Zavodovski Island had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic Peninsula to 5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity Peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4°C, about 20°C above normal for the time of year — a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy.”
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30 percent — though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “ Penguin Pompeii hypothesis ” of a sudden population fall, this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

articles.content_orig:
The World’s Largest Pet Walk encourages the public to enjoy the health benefits of walking with pets.
After being postponed last month due to Hurricane Nolo, the World’s Largest Pet Walk has been rescheduled for 8 a.m. this Saturday in Waimea.
The World’s Largest Pet Walk encourages the public to enjoy the health benefits of being active with pets.
Community members and their pets are welcome to join Queen’s North Hawaii Community Hospital’s pet therapy teams on a two-mile walk starting across from Pukalani Stables at 8 a.m., rain or shine.
Pets must be well-behaved and on leashes. No sign up is required, and walkers without pets are welcomed. For questions, please call 881-4421.
This special pet walk was created by Pet Partners, the nation’s leading organization registering therapy animals.
Walking daily can increase cardiovascular fitness and reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke. In addition, research has found that people who walk with an animal are more likely to meet physical activity recommendations.
“The World’s Largest Pet Walk is a wonderful opportunity to come together as a community while celebrating the special bond between people and animals,” Lynn Scully, spokeswoman for QNHCH, said in a press release. “Bring your pet, or enjoy the walk with one of our friendly therapy animals. Anyone interested in becoming a therapy animal team can learn more at petpartners.org or visit the hospital’s website at www.nhch.com (Careers/Career Paths/Volunteer).”

articles.title_orig: A Volkswagen bestseller goes electric: world premiere of the new ID. Tiguan
articles.title_zh: A Volkswagen bestseller goes electric: world premiere of the new ID. Tiguan
articles.content_orig:
Volkswagen presents the new ID. Tiguan, one of the brand’s most important electric models for the years ahead. The new all-round SUV in the high-volume mid-size class succeeds the ID.4 and ID.5 models. The ID. Tiguan’s hallmark feature is its completely redesigned exterior, which gives it the appearance of a vehicle from the next class up. And this impression continues seamlessly into the strikingly high-quality interior: the materials used have resulted in a huge leap forwards in terms of quality, complemented by the newly developed, intuitive cockpit landscape. For the first time, the new SUV will be available with a co-driver display . The electrically powered ID. Tiguan will be launched as early as the beginning of 2027 – in parallel to the current Tiguan with petrol, diesel and hybrid drives.
Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the Volkswagen brand, Head of the Brand Group Core and member of the Group Board of Management: “The Tiguan is our  best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most  successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success  stories together. A pure, confident design with the presence of a  vehicle from the next class up, intuitive operation and, thanks to MEB+,  a range of up to 600 kilometres : a new  benchmark for our electric SUVs made in Germany. Together with the  Tiguan from Wolfsburg, the ID. Tiguan from Emden is part of one of the  strongest SUV duos in Europe.”
Range of up to 600 km and a maximum towing capacity of 2,000 kg. Volkswagen will offer the ID. Tiguan in three performance levels:
Depending on the power and battery size, the WLTP ranges will reach up to 600 km . At the same time, the model impresses with its high suitability for everyday use: the towing capacity is up to 1,800 kg with the 58 kWh battery, and up to 2,000 kg with the 77 kWh battery. In addition, there is a frunk with 32 litres of stowage space and a luggage compartment volume of up to 534 litres. Functional, comfortable or sporty: the ID. Tiguan will be available in the four equipment versions Trend, Life, Style and R-Line.
Progress visible everywhere. Volkswagen has specifically incorporated customer requests into the development of the new ID. Tiguan, implementing countless enhancements and advanced technologies. Taking the cockpit landscape as an example, highlights include a co-driver display (12-inch, 30.5-cm diagonal), the first time a feature like this has appeared in a European Volkswagen. The 10-inch driver display (Digital Cockpit, 25.4-cm diagonal) and the central 15-inch infotainment display (38.1-cm diagonal) are also new. Together with the co-driver display, this results in a continuous display landscape that opens up a new world, especially for the front passenger – one where they can immerse themselves in their own world of infotainment, information, and gaming without distracting the driver. This is because the display is not visible to the driver, as with a laptop privacy screen (privacy mode). In privacy mode, the front passenger can listen to the sound on their paired Bluetooth headphones.
The ID. Tiguan embodies a new design language. One of Volkswagen’s core values is a superior and timeless design. And this is embodied in every way by the new ID. Tiguan. The Pure Positive design language has a major influence on the exterior design of the ID. Tiguan: the softer crossover design of the predecessors has given way to a powerful SUV design with a strong visual presence. Precise lines and tightly sculpted surfaces lend it additional stability and quality. As a result, the new model looks like a vehicle from the premium segment. In addition, Volkswagen is returning to classic pull-style door handles with the ID. Tiguan.
On a premium level. The interior also boasts a clear, high-quality design, intuitive controls, a  premium feel and an atmosphere that is welcoming in every respect. This  feeling is reinforced by elegant lighting effects. The interplay of  design, materials and a stylish colour scheme creates an atmosphere  reminiscent of the next segment above.
Intuitive operation. Volkswagen has implemented a clear operating logic throughout the ID. Tiguan. Important functions can therefore be accessed using physical buttons again and have been incorporated into the interior where you would intuitively expect to find them. The air conditioning system is a prime example of this: the basic functions are now controlled via a button bar in the centre console. The door openers in the interior are another example: they are ergonomically optimised to sit perfectly in the hand. In this area on the driver’s side, the in-door control panel for the four power windows has also been redesigned. A further example is the process for adjusting the audio volume and changing the station/track, which is performed primarily using an intuitively accessible controller in the centre console. Positioned at the front: two inductive charging points compliant with the Qi2 standard; integrated magnetic rings position and secure compatible smartphones precisely on the charging points. Another new feature is the multifunction steering wheel with physical buttons instead of touch controls.
New ‘Retro’ displays. In spite of all the focus on functionality, there is also an element of fun as demonstrated by the ‘Retro’ displays. These are a brand-new development for the ID. Tiguan. If the driver activates the ‘Retro’ display using the ‘View’ button on the multifunction steering wheel, the iconic blue-red instruments from a Golf IV appear in the Digital Cockpit. In this case, there is a classic speedometer on the left and a stylised rev counter on the right. It does not display engine speeds but the energy flow in the drive as a power display. The corresponding ‘Retro’ view in the central infotainment screen can also be personalised for the first time. Here, the driver can choose from six different Volkswagen models, which are displayed in a virtual garage: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg and Beetle.
Innovative technologies, optional equipment. Modern assistance, driving and comfort systems are available for the new ID.   Tiguan. These include features such as the standard-equipment one-pedal   driving (strong deceleration using the accelerator pedal alone), the  new  Connected Travel Assist , which, among  other  things, enables assisted lane changing on motorways and automatically stops  the  ID. Tiguan at red traffic lights .
In addition, comfort features  such as  electrically adjustable front seats with  massage, memory and ventilation functions as well as  a high-end sound  system from Harman Kardon  with an output of 480  watts and a panoramic sunroof will be part of  the optional equipment range.
Well thought-out down to the last detail. A practical and flexible feature is the Digital Key . This enables the vehicle to be unlocked, locked and  started using a compatible smartphone. The Digital Key can also be  transferred to family members, friends or colleagues – using the  Volkswagen app, it can be shared easily by means of text message,  messenger services or email. Another clever and practical solution is  the PowerSocket for Vehicle-to-Load. This  adapter is simply plugged into the charging socket of the ID. Tiguan and  can be used to power all kinds of electrical devices – from electric  grills to e-bikes.

FILE-A detailed view of Apple's new iPhone 18 Pro at Apple Regent Street on September 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by George Mattock/Getty Images)
Apple is slashing orders for its newly launched iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max as surging memory chip costs and price increases have lowered consumer demand for the devices.
The company has taken a different approach on shipments of the iPhones since September, with component orders ​for October being cut roughly 15%, according to Reuters, citing a Nikkei Asia report.
In September, Apple debuted the latest generation of its flagship smartphone, with the iPhone 18 Pro and the 18 Pro Max ​handsets, alongside its foldable phone duo.
The iPhone 18 Pro ​and ⁠Pro Max start at $1,199 and $1,299, up $100 from the starting prices of the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max.
RELATED: Apple unveils foldable iPhone called Duo, iPhone 18 Pro lineup
Forbes reported that the iPhone 18 Pro models won’t be Apple’s flagship smartphone launch for 2026. Last month, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, a passport-sized phone with an inner screen that folds out to a size that is like the iPad Mini.
Reuters noted that demand for Apple devices has dwindled from late August into October, but that could be connected to the tech giant changing its launch schedule ​for iPhone models.
Meanwhile, with the addition of more AI features to the iPhone and other Apple devices, the company’s demand for high-performance memory has surged, raising the role of suppliers amid a global shortage.

articles.content_orig:

Just when you thought the sun might be taking a breather, it's unleashed another powerful eruption — and the northern lights forecast just got even more promising.
A fourth coronal mass ejection (CME) erupted from the sun on Oct. 8, during a powerful M-class solar flare from the restless sunspot region AR4549. That brings the number of CMEs potentially heading Earth's way to four, raising the possibility of further geomagnetic activity and aurora displays over the coming days.
Early analysis suggests the latest CME could potentially catch up with the third CME on its way towards Earth.
NOAA's aurora forecast suggests auroral activity could be enhanced across northern North America. Exactly how far south the aurora might appear remains uncertain and depends on how the incoming CMEs interact with Earth's magnetic field .
G2 geomagnetic storm conditions are forecast for Oct. 9 and during such storms, auroras have previously been observed as far south as New York and Idaho .
While northern U.S. states currently have the best prospects, skywatchers farther south shouldn't completely write off their chances just yet. With multiple CMEs approaching Earth in quick succession, there's still considerable uncertainty over how geomagnetic conditions will develop. If the incoming eruptions interact favorably with Earth's magnetic field, auroras could potentially reach much farther south than currently anticipated.
So if you're at mid-latitudes, make sure those aurora alerts are switched on and your camera batteries are charged. This could be an interesting few days for northern lights enthusiasts!
For real-time forecasts based on your location, consider using a space weather app. A great option is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts" (available for iOS and Android ). For a deeper dive into space weather conditions, "Space Weather Live" is another excellent choice (available for iOS and Android )
NOAA's latest 3-day forecast now places the strongest geomagnetic activity later on Oct. 9 than previously anticipated.
Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions are forecast between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. EDT (1200and 1800 GMT), with moderate (G2) conditions predicted between 2 and 8 p.m. EDT (1800 and midnight GMT) .
Further activity is possible over the weekend, with NOAA currently forecasting minor (G1) conditions between 11 p.m. and 2 a.m. EDT on Oct. 10-11 (0300-0600 GMT Oct. 11).
For those wishing to catch some auroras, the advice remains the same! Keep your aurora alerts switched on and check conditions whenever skies are dark and clear. These forecast windows are not set in stone, particularly when multiple CMEs are involved!
This is where things get complicated.
Current modelling suggests the first CMEs could reach Earth on Oct. 9. Space weather physicist Tamitha Skov notes that the two Oct. 6 CMEs could reach Earth in relatively quick succession, delivering a one-two punch to Earth's magnetic field. However, their journey may be influenced by the surrounding solar wind , making precise arrival times difficult to pin down.
The third CME could follow late Oct. 10 or early Oct. 11 (UTC), potentially prolonging unsettled geomagnetic activity and aurora prospects into the weekend.
And now there's a fourth CME to consider. Early analysis suggests this latest eruption is traveling faster than some of its predecessors, raising the possibility that it could catch up with the third CME before reaching Earth. The 'cannibal CME' could further complicate the timings and strength of resulting geomagnetic activity. And remember, even an Earth-directed CME doesn't guarantee a spectacular aurora display. Much will depend on how the magnetic fields carried by these eruptions interact with Earth's magnetic field when they arrive.
With AR4549 still magnetically complex and facing Earth, more solar activity could be on the way. The sun sure is keeping us on our toes this week!
Editor's note: This article has been updated to include a fourth coronal mass ejection (CME) that erupted from the sun on Oct. 8, along with the latest geomagnetic storm forecasts and revised arrival estimates.
Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.
Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.
She will be a guest speaker aboard HX's Solar Eclipse Expedition in August 2026 and will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

articles.title_orig: Poll: 1 in 4 Trump voters say GOP candidates should break from the president
articles.title_zh: Poll: 1 in 4 Trump voters say GOP candidates should break from the president
articles.content_orig:
It has become abundantly clear that Republicans in tough races aren’t especially eager to campaign with President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm election.
Few of them showed up to Trump’s midterm convention last month. His travel schedule since then has rather curiously featured lower-tier states like Alabama, Oklahoma and New York and only a handful of real battleground races. And even in Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott is skipping Trump’s upcoming rally (citing scheduling conflicts, of course).
Trump increasingly appears rather sensitive about this dynamic — which makes sense, given he’s latched onto the theory that he alone can push his party to victory in less than four weeks, despite his low approval numbers.
He went on a tear about his rallies on Tuesday, bringing it up at least five separate times.
“By the way, I’m going around doing rallies. The Republican Party is starting to go right through the roof,” he said at a non-campaign event in Baltimore. “Somebody said today, ‘I wonder why?’ Well, I started — I had to get out. I had to do it.”
(There is no evidence Trump’s rallies are actually helping, which we’ll get to.)
He posted on social media that his “Rally crowds and enthusiasm are unbelievable!” He added: “ We are flipping races all over the place . … It’s all happening!”
In a separate post, he said simply: “ MY RALLIES ARE SAVING THE REPUBLICAN PARTY, AGAIN!!! ”
In gaggles with reporters, he returned to the topic even when he wasn’t asked about it, claiming at one point that “the rallies have changed things around.” When asked about leaked audio of Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton saying DC was controlling his campaign, Trump responded that Paxton was “doing much better” since Trump started doing rallies a few days ago.
And when a reporter asked Monday about campaigning in Michigan, Trump said he would. When asked about campaigning in Maine, he suggested he would go there, too.
“I don’t know about Maine,” Trump said. “I think we’re going to Maine, too.”
But GOP Sen. Susan Collins has said repeatedly — including at a debate Tuesday night — that she didn’t expect Trump to come to Maine. “That’s just not going to happen,” Collins said in June .
This is also an uneasy question in Iowa, where three House Republicans recently broke from Trump somewhat on the Iran war. And Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson seems to want some distance from Trump.
When those lawmakers were at a White House event last week, Trump seemed to put them on the spot, bringing up plans for more campaign events with him.
“I’m going to come to Iowa,” Trump said, adding: “I will say that we’re going to do a great rally, and we’ll all be there together. We have to get you all elected.”
Hinson responded: “We’ll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir.”
And back in early September, when it became clear many Republicans in marquee races were skipping the president’s Trump-centric midterm convention, the president claimed it was for reasons beside his historically low poll numbers.
“Everybody wants to come,” Trump maintained, adding: “The reason that some people are not coming is because we don’t have room for 500 politicians.”
He also said back then that he would be all over the country, campaigning for every Republican in the most competitive races.
“I’m going to go to every one of those 35 places, and we’re going to see if we can get everyone elected,” he said September 2. He repeated the same claim at the convention a week later: “I’m gonna go to every one of them, about 35. In a couple of cases, I’ll go twice.”
That doesn’t appear to be happening anymore — at least not yet. With less than four weeks to go, Trump has been to only a handful of true battleground areas.
And despite Trump’s claim that he’s such an asset, it appears that his “Trump-a-palooza” midterm convention backfired on Republicans. Polls show the generic ballot, a key measure of the midterm, took a turn in Democrats’ favor at almost that precise moment.
Of course, Trump simply can’t allow for this perception that Republicans don’t want to campaign with him and that he’s an electoral burden.
His ability to rally the base at raucous, large-scale events has been a central part of his political brand, yet he’s confronting a reality where many Republicans seem to view them as net-negatives.
The lack of Republicans pining to campaign with him also calls into question his domination of his party, which he has been cultivating for a decade and is central to his hold on what political capital he has left. If he truly lost the base and his ability to make Republicans do what he wants, he wouldn’t have much left.
In the four-week span left before the election, it could become abundantly clear just how many Republicans think Trump is an albatross and a lame duck.
So he’s over-compensating for that — badly.

articles.title_orig: Mélenchon declares ‘Bastille retaken’ after major student rally in Paris
articles.title_zh: Mélenchon declares ‘Bastille retaken’ after major student rally in Paris
articles.content_orig:
France has been struggling to contain its biggest student protests in decades .
The protests started last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb, where students joined their striking teachers to protest a lack of staff and resources. When their demands were met and extra staff were sent to the school, the strike ended.
But shortly after that, students in Paris and the surrounding region began blocking entrances to their schools. Within days, similar scenes were reported across the country. Images of students setting alight trash cans, manning barricades, assaulting teaching staff and clashing with police have led to questions about the police’s response and the far left’s involvement.
Hundreds of schools have been forced to close, and thousands of people have been taken into police custody over the past few weeks — most of them minors with no previous criminal records.
Critics have accused the police of a heavy-handed response. Following a massive day of protests on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron demanded “empathy” from police forces facing student protesters.
In an address to the nation Wednesday, French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said parliament next month would debate a budget proposal that includes 64 billion euros ($71.6 billion) in funding for education, a slight increase from last year. He also said the government has launched five initiatives to respond to students’ needs.
But there has been little sign that school blockades will halt in the meantime. Student unions have called for a day of protests on October 17.
Here are some of the stories that made headlines over the past week, as well as some photos that caught our eye.

articles.title_orig: House Republicans are bracing for catastrophe in once safe red seats
articles.title_zh: House Republicans are bracing for catastrophe in once safe red seats
articles.content_orig:
Scores of House Republicans are preparing for the worst-case scenario after internal polling showed just how doomed the GOP could be in the midterms, according to a report.
Senior Republicans, House GOP leadership, and those involved in individual campaigns are in full panic mode after receiving damning numbers in late September that suggest even races in red areas of states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024 are in danger .
Sources told Politico the internal polling didnât reveal the usual problems a ruling party faces in a midterm year but instead pointed to âclose-to-catastrophic scenariosâ in what should be considered safe red seats across the country.
âI think the scary part is we donât know where the bottom is,â one senior House Republican told the outlet.
A midterm âblue waveâ against Donald Trump could be even worse than already expected.
The Republican Party is widely expected to lose control of the House in the midterms, as the party in power has historically suffered major losses in the lower chamber and the GOP currently has only a razor-thin majority.
However, voter backlash against Trumpâs turbulent second term, including the war in Iran and his dire handling of the economy, could mean that key House seats previously not considered at risk in states such as Kentucky, North Carolina, and Nevada could be in play for Democrats in November.
Trump and the GOPâs midterm strategy suggest they are increasingly worried about losing red House seats, on top of facing challenges in key competitive races.
By clicking â SUBSCRIBE â you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy .
The president is spending a significant amount of time in the crucial run-up to the Nov. 3 elections campaigning for candidates in red states such as Texas and Oklahoma.
On Saturday, Trump will appear in Tennesseeâa state he won in 2024 by 30 pointsâin GOP Rep. Matt Van Eppsâ district. While Van Eppsâ seat is still considered safe, some Republicans fear a shock could be in store because of intense backlash against the president.
âIâm worried about all three in the area,â one Tennessee Republican told Politico of the red-leaning districts. âToo many unknowns.â
Trump is headed to Tennessee this weekend, where Rep. Matt Van Epps is in a tougher than expected race for re-election.
Brett Carlsen/Getty Images
Internal polling also shows that all three Republican candidates in Iowaâincumbent Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and Joe Mitchell, the GOP candidate seeking to replace Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senateâcould lose their races.
Other incumbents facing tighter-than-desired races include Wisconsin Rep. Bryan Steil, who won his 2024 election by 11 points, and Minnesota Rep. Brad Finstad, who won his district by 12 points in 2024.
Mike Johnson is not expected to still be House speaker at the start of the next congressional term.
Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images
âPeople that are in R+10 districts are showing [polling that] theyâre tied and theyâre saying, âI need help,ââ a GOP operative working on a battleground House race told Politico. âThereâs real opportunity for Democrats in a lot of these.â
A spokesperson for the Republican National Committee rejected suggestions that major panic was setting in ahead of the midterms.
âAnonymous strategists who spend more time bed-wetting to media than working in the trenches to win races have no idea what theyâre talking about,â RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Politico.
National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Mike Marinella added: âHouse Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, a historic fundraising and spending advantages, and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.â
The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

articles.title_orig: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.title_zh: Finland: The world's happiest nation faces a glum winter
articles.content_orig:
There's an uneasy mood in Finland , the country that's ranked the world's happiest for nine consecutive years . A colder-than-usual winter is on the way and so is the toughest austerity budget in years.
With an election due in April, the argument is no longer how much to cut, but which services, benefits and pensions will face the biggest cuts.
Finland's debt and deficit levels are in their worst state since the 1990s, when a banking crash and the collapse of the Soviet Union — a key export partner — pushed the Nordic nation into its own Great Depression.
Last month, Finland's national statistical institution confirmed that the national debt had reached 90.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter. Before the pandemic, that figure was around 65%.
Trouble to the east is, again, part of the reason. Finland ramped up defense spending after joining NATO a year after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Helsinki, which used to rely on Moscow for about a third of its energy, also faced much higher costs as it transitioned to other suppliers.
The Finnish government has spent more than it earns since the 2008/9 global financial crisis, partly due to an aging population and sluggish economic growth. Last month, the State Treasury projected the fiscal deficit would reach 4.2% of GDP in 2026.
Brussels has piled pressure on Helsinki to bring down the borrowing gap, as European Union rules require member states to stay below 3% of GDP. In January, the European Council opened an excessive deficit procedure and gave Finland until the end of 2028 to reach the desired target.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's government, which took office in June 2023, said it would aim to save about €9 billion ($10.1 billion) during this parliamentary term. But whoever wins the next election will have to cut much deeper, economists warn.
"The amounts currently estimated range from €8 to €11 billion," Jarkko Kivisto, an advisor to the Bank of Finland's monetary policy and research department, told DW.
Earlier this year, all but one political party agreed to support a debt brake, where the next government commits to tightening the country's deficit to about 2% of GDP by 2031.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
To date, Orpo's center-right National Coalition is the only party to promise a further €9 billion in cuts if he wins a second term. As well as further savings from health, social care and welfare, Orpo also plans to target workplace pensions, without reducing current payouts.
While the Social Democrats plan to split the reforms between spending cuts and tax hikes, Orpo plans to achieve his target without raising taxes — meaning public services will bear the brunt.
Kivisto, however, cautioned: "The deficit is so large that it would need a package that includes tax increases and expenditure cuts."
While Finland's at-risk-of-poverty rate is lower than the EU average, unemployment is higher than anywhere else in the bloc. In August, Finland's jobless total stood at 10.3%, just above Spain's 10%, according to Eurostat, the bloc's statistics agency. Youth unemployment reached 23.3%, against an EU average of 15.4%.
With household spending already falling, Lauri Holappa, director of the Finnish Centre for New Economic Analysis, warned that a new round of austerity would be a hard blow for the domestic economy.
"More than a quarter of the population works in the public sector, so if those workers face the threat of being sacked, the savings rate will rise and private spending will drop again," Holappa told DW.
Successive pressures ranging from the COVID-19 pandemic, higher interest rates and the global financial impact of two current wars have hurt efforts to cut the growing gap between income and borrowing. The 2027 budget proposal still counts on a spending gap of €12.4 billion.
Before the Ukraine war, Finland had already committed to buying 64 F-35A fighter jets from the United States, in a deal worth about €8.4 billion.
During more than four years of Russia's war in Ukraine, the Nordic nation raised military spending from $4.5 billion to over $8 billion per year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
In April, the government said it would further increase defense spending to 3.2% of GDP, close to NATO's 3.5% target.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
With oil prices remaining close to $100 a barrel due to the Iran war , the government has so far resisted pressure to increase fuel subsidies. That's despite the Bank of Finland recording a 50% rise in the cost of imported energy in the early months of the Iran war.
While Finland’s shift to renewables, along with the opening of the Olkiluoto 3 nuclear power plant in 2023, has helped avoid a worse energy crisis, the central bank warned this summer that sustained high oil and gas prices would mean "lower economic growth and higher inflation" next year.
On another positive note, parts of Finland's export sector are booming, thanks to strong metal and shipbuilding orders, which Holappa described as strong as "the boom years of Nokia," when the once market-leading phone maker carried Finnish economic growth.
"There is a possibility that the export sector can steer us out of this recession," he told DW, as long as demand from the rest of Europe remains strong.
Despite the multiple roadblocks to bringing down the deficit, market reaction to Finland's debt woes has, so far, been muted. Rating agencies have kept the country's outlook stable, apart from S&P, which turned negative in April without cutting the rating.
On October 6, the premium the Finnish government pays over Germany to borrow for 10 years was 38 basis points. That compares to 128 for France and 107 for Italy. In other words, investors still treat Finnish debt as among the safest in Europe.
That is, as long as the next shock is not another extended oil-price spike, a fresh escalation from Russia, or a Europe-wide debt crisis centered on France.
Next March, Finland could still be named the planet's happiest nation for the 10th year in a row. How long the smiles last, once the bill for decades of borrowing arrives a month later, is anyone's guess.

articles.title_orig: A Nobel for chiral catalysts’ helping hand
articles.title_zh: A Nobel for chiral catalysts’ helping hand
articles.content_orig:
By Phillip Broadwith 2026-10-09T08:05:00+01:00
The 2026 Nobel prize in chemistry has been awarded to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai , ‘for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis’. The prize recognises the pair’s contribution to understanding the very fundamentals of how we can influence and control the handedness of chiral molecules.
Asymmetric synthesis is a cornerstone of modern drug development, as well as being important for flavours, fragrances and agrochemicals. But chiral molecules also crop up in liquid crystals, polymers and optical materials, as well as across various classes of speciality chemicals. Almost all these products rely, at some point, on catalysts that can transform achiral or racemic molecules into products in which one enantiomer is massively – if not exclusively – dominant.
Source: © Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images
This year’s prize recognises truly fundamental science that has had huge bearing on the commercial applications of asymmetric catalysis
When you’re aiming to make chiral molecules for commercial sale, an efficient synthesis has a significant effect on cost – and hence profitability. Cleaner reactions mean less wasted materials, as well as less time and resources spent on separation and purification. Understanding how to create more effective catalysts, which can drive higher yields and selectivity, can translate into a huge competitive advantage.
Henri Kagan and his team’s insight into the intricacies of how catalysts can be manipulated to drastically improve their performance underlies all this development. Likewise, there are different approaches to enantio-enrichment, as Kenso Soai and his team’s autocatalytic experiments showed.
This year’s laureates didn’t invent asymmetric synthesis, but filled in some key aspects in our understanding of how it works and how we can do it better. This fundamental research has naturally stimulated many other researchers to ask further questions, digging deeper into how these reactions work and further advancing our understanding of chirality and catalysis.
That, in turn, shows up in the applications: new and better catalyst systems have allowed us to build ever more complex molecules in more efficient ways, and directly enabled the wide commercial availability of chiral reagents and chemical building blocks. A fact that’s worth remembering next time you’re browsing through a catalogue, planning your next synthesis.

articles.title_orig: Scrapped IPO of Nvidia-Backed Company Points to Limits of AI Boom
articles.title_zh: Scrapped IPO of Nvidia-Backed Company Points to Limits of AI Boom
articles.content_orig:
Australian AI data center operator Firmus, which is backed by Nvidia , has withdrawn its planned mega initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions, the company said in an emailed statement to CNBC.
Firmus said its board determined that the terms of the proposed offering did not adequately reflect the strength of its business and long-term growth outlook.
"The board therefore concluded that proceeding with the offer was not in the best interests of the company and its shareholders," Firmus said in a statement. "Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options," it added.
Firmus had reportedly planned to raise $5 billion in its IPO, pricing shares at A$11 apiece, which would have made it the second-largest new share sale in Australia's history. The IPO valued the company at around $30.6 billion.
In August, the company announced a $2 billion funding round backed by Nvidia, Coatue Management, Blackstone and Jane Street, bringing its total equity raised over the preceding year to more than $3 billion and its valuation to over $10.5 billion.
Firmus also announced agreements with Meta last month to provide GPU computing capacity at its AI data centers in Southeast Asia, built on Nvidia's DSX platform, to support Meta's AI research, model development and training.

But OneDrive storage is being cut to a shared 2TB pool across all family members.
But OneDrive storage is being cut to a shared 2TB pool across all family members.
Microsoft bundled its AI-powered Office features into Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscriptions last year , but it only allowed the primary account holder to access the AI benefits. Now, Microsoft is about to let Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers share Copilot and AI usage features, alongside access to Office apps and OneDrive storage, with up to five other people on a plan.
In an email to Microsoft 365 Family and Premium subscribers seen by The Verge , Microsoft outlines the changes that are coming to subscription plans over the coming months:
The storage changes seem like the major downside to Microsoft’s updates. Instead of getting 1TB of OneDrive storage per account, Microsoft is now limiting this to just 2TB of shared storage across the entire plan. Microsoft argues this makes storage more flexible if one member exceeds 1TB, but it looks like it’s an easy way for the company to upsell more OneDrive storage in reality.
According to a support note , “Existing subscribers in eligible markets might also qualify for transitional bonus storage.” Microsoft is also planning to provide support to families that use a lot of storage
The changes are being announced a year after Microsoft 365 Premium launched , which offers all the benefits of a Copilot Pro and a Microsoft 365 Family subscription for $19.99 a month. The “more flexible AI usage” change could mean that some subscribers end up paying more for AI usage, depending on how they’re using Copilot.

articles.title_orig: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.title_zh: World Bank and IMF’s lack of climate action could make countries bystanders in their own destruction
articles.content_orig:
© World Economic Forum / Benedikt von Loebell
The World Bank and IMF are shifting away from explicit climate action towards resilience, reflecting political pressure from the US that weakens their response to global heating, argues Federico Sibaja  and Jon Sward.
The authors criticise the World Bank’s approach after its financing supported a Nepal hydropower project that was damaged by devastating floods despite warnings and the absence of a proper climate-risk assessment.
Meanwhile, IMF-backed austerity and fossil-fuel policies in countries including Ecuador and Pakistan are limiting investment in climate adaptation and, in some cases, undermining the shift to renewable energy.
With climate-vulnerable countries facing mounting damage, the authors argue that institutions must expand grant-based finance and debt relief, and ensure climate risks are built into lending decisions and economic programmes.
In a recent interview with the New York Times , World Bank President Ajay Banga explained that the bank wants to avoid the “emotional” debate around climate change and instead focus on resilient investments.
For the leader of an institution that describes itself as the “knowledge bank”, such a desire to skirt the realities of climate science is of course the result of political calculus.
The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, has also shifted gears in recent years: she went from calling for an end to “business as usual” at COP28 , to agreeing with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on the need to refocus away from climate change. She has also cut the budget earmarked for climate work by 27%.
Meanwhile, Bessent has questioned the cause of global warming and referred to climate action at global financial institutions as driven by “elite beliefs” .
The World Bank and IMF’s change in approach comes as no surprise, as there is a potentially steep cost of them falling afoul of their largest shareholder, amid its wider war on multilateralism.
But what’s been less discussed is the wider cost of the Bretton Woods institutions’ failure to act in the midst of an accelerating climate emergency – of which the serious flooding in Bangkok, where the World Bank and IMF convene their annual meetings next week, is a stark reminder.
After a prolonged debate on the future of the bank’s climate commitments in the Spring, a compromise was reached in June , when it extended its climate change action plan (CCAP) “indefinitely”, but retired its 45% climate finance target.
As the US’s anti-climate action agenda has cast a long shadow at the institution and elsewhere since last year, bank officials increasingly say their goal is to deliver resilient investments, echoing Banga’s recent statements.
However, there are serious questions about whether the bank’s approach is advancing its aim.
The recent flood disaster in Nepal, which killed more than 1,450 people (with around 5,800 still missing), also damaged 13 hydropower projects, including the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower plant. Alongside other lenders , Trishuli was backed by financing from the World Bank’s private investment arm , IFC, and a US$87.4mn guarantee from its political risk arm, MIGA. Yet, despite repeated warnings from an independent expert panel, no climate and disaster risk assessment had been properly undertaken as of 2024.
The World Bank needs to ensure that “resilience” is more than an empty signifier. This means having mechanisms in place across all lending instruments to evaluate whether its actions are genuinely leading to positive outcomes for people and the planet, including ex-post assessments of projects that emphasise learning from past mistakes.
It also means rethinking the the bank’s neoliberal era loan conditions in its policy based lending , which have promoted wholesale privatisation in key sectors like energy, and ensuring countries have the policy and fiscal space to pursue green industrial policy .
As evidenced by the Nepal crisis, with the country facing an estimated US$4.7bn in reconstruction costs, climate-vulnerable countries also urgently need a rapid scaling up of grant-based climate finance and debt relief . The World Bank could use its convening role to help move this discussion forward.
The IMF’s relevance has grown due to increasingly frequent shocks to the global economy, such as spikes in fossil fuel prices and extreme weather events. In July 2026 , 30 countries were implementing IMF programmes with conditionalities, and 14 other countries were seeking new arrangements.
Recent analysis has shown that its programmes’ reliance on fiscal consolidation and foreign exchange accumulation can undermine countries’ climate policy goals and put macroeconomic stability – Bessent’s  “focus” of the IMF – at risk. So, while the IMF has become better at diagnosing climate risk, it is also exacerbating it.
For example, in Ecuador, the IMF-backed programme requires primary adjustment of 6.6% of GDP. Such fiscal adjustment can make it harder to invest in climate adaptation and resilient infrastructure. At the same time, the programme explicitly aims to increase oil output.
The same goes for Pakistan. The country has been on the frontlines of the climate crisis in the last few years, with devastating floods in 2022. Yet IMF-backed fiscal consolidation has constrained spending at a time when the country faces enormous adaptation needs. Moreover, reforms in fiscal policy are undermining the energy transition: due to IMF-led energy subsidy removal and tariff increases, the country began a rapid shift to solar, only to see it undermined by IMF-backed higher taxes on solar panels.
Back in June, the IMF’s own independent evaluation office flagged this contradiction. It identified the review of progam design and conditionality , the process through which the institution evaluates the performance of its lending programmes and agrees ways to improve them, as a chance to address it. Yet, when the review wrapped up last month, climate was firmly excluded .
As more countries turn to the IMF to address their vulnerability to shocks, its push for fiscal adjustment and commodity extraction risks accelerating that same vulnerability.
At the upcoming annual meetings, we need to see serious efforts to resolve this contradiction. A good place to start would be the guidance the IMF provides to staff designing loan programmes, which will be developed in the next few months. This must clearly outline under what circumstances climate goals are central to programme success and cannot be ignored.
Without a change of course, the IMF and World Bank will miss a key window of opportunity to stem a runaway climate crisis. In the present context, delaying action is just another form of climate denial.
This page was last updated October 9, 2026
Federico Sibaja is the lead for Fair International Financial System work at Recourse. An economist from the Universidad de Buenos Aires, he is an expert on the interactions between debt and climate policy. He has extensive experience in policymaking, research and campaigning across Argentina, Belgium and internationally.
Jon Sward is environment project manager at the Bretton Woods Project, where he oversees its climate advocacy work towards the World Bank and the IMF. He holds a PhD from the School of Global Studies at the University of Sussex.

articles.title_orig: PEI Group reveals the world's 100 biggest private markets firms have raised $5.74 trillion in five years
articles.title_zh: PEI Group reveals the world's 100 biggest private markets firms have raised $5.74 trillion in five years
articles.content_orig:
PEI Group's ground-breaking Private Markets 100 report measures private equity, real estate, infrastructure, private credit and secondaries together for the first time.
LONDON , Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The 100 largest private markets managers raised $5.74 trillion between 2021 and 2025, more than the annual economic output of Germany*, according to the inaugural Private Markets 100 published by PEI Group.
Blackstone heads the ranking at $356.7 billion, KKR is second at $302.2 billion and Goldman Sachs Alternatives third at $215.3 billion.
The top 10 raised $2.04 trillion between them, 35.5 percent of the total.
PEI Private Markets 100 top 10
Goldman Sachs Alternatives
Brookfield Asset Management
The specialist is disappearing
PEI Group is the first business intelligence firm to provide a five-year global fundraising ranking across the five major asset classes, bringing together data from PEI's well-known industry standard rankings which investors trust and rely on.
Measuring the five asset classes together in this way shows what separate rankings cannot: the biggest managers are no longer single asset class specialists.
Sixteen of the top 100 firms in the ranking raised money across all five strategies, and seven of the top 10 are active in all five, while a quarter of the list (25 firms) made the top 100 by being active in a single asset class.
Ares Management shows the largest shift in a single year. It raised more private credit than any other firm, moved from 10 th to fourth in real estate and from 16 th to 10 th in secondaries. Added together, that makes it the fifth-largest private markets fundraiser in the world, ahead of both Brookfield and BlackRock.
Much of the convergence is being bought rather than built. In the past two years KKR has acquired sports investor Arctos Partners, EQT has acquired secondaries firm Coller Capital for up to $3.7 billion, and Goldman Sachs has bought Industry Ventures. General Atlantic has acquired infrastructure manager Actis and BNP Paribas has completed its purchase of AXA Investment Managers.
"The industry has outgrown its own categories," said Dan Gunner, Director of Research at PEI Group . "Firms that were buyout houses 10 years ago now raise more for credit than for equity. By methodically analysing and launching the first ever PEI Private Markets 100, we are offering a complete view of the wider market which allows the industry to see the full fundraising picture like never before. This is testimony to the unmatched capability we bring in Research and Analysis, and the breadth and depth of the data we have across private markets, which stretches back over more than 15 years."
* Germany nominal GDP, 2025 $5.01trn (IMF World Economic Outlook, Oct 2025)
Understanding the PEI Private Markets 100
The PEI Private Markets 100 ranks managers by capital raised for private markets funds over the five years to 31 December 2025. It consolidates PEI Group's six established asset class rankings, each compiled annually from manager submissions and validated against public filings, regulatory disclosures and fund documentation. A manager needed $18.97 billion to make the list. Figures are amounts raised, not assets under management. Where a fund invests across strategies its capital is split between rankings rather than counted twice.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices fall as Trump pauses Iran attacks, China restarts fuel exports – business live
articles.title_zh: Oil prices fall as Trump pauses Iran attacks, China restarts fuel exports – business live
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices rose sharply Thursday, as Iran ramped up its attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz and Hurricane Isaias threatened U.S. offshore production in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, gained 4% to close at $104.28 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 3.6% to settle at $91.49 per barrel.
Nine tankers have come under attack in and around Hormuz over the past week, jeopardizing the recent recovery in crude oil flows through the strait
Oil prices backed off session highs after President Donald Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November midterm elections. NBC News, citing unnamed sources, reported earlier that Trump and his national security team were considering renewing strikes in the coming weeks.
Some 9.5 million barrels per day exited Hormuz during the week ended Tuesday, about 30% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to Kpler data. Crude flows from the Middle East, including pipeline workarounds, stood at 16.4 million bpd which is nearly equivalent to prewar levels.
In the Gulf of Mexico, oil companies have shut in about 500,000 bpd, or 25% of offshore production in the region, as Hurricane Isaias churns toward the coasts of Alabama, Mississippi and the Florida panhandle.
Tensions are sharply escalating in the Middle East. Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen fired missiles at airports in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and the city of Abha on Tuesday and Wednesday. Three people died and 36 were injured, according to the state-owned media outlet Al Arabiya.
The Saudis intercepted another volley of ballistic missiles fired Thursday at Riyadh and Khamis Mushait, a spokesperson for the kingdom's military said.
"While flows from the region have largely normalized, the need for US navy escorts, increased costs and logistical frictions and constant risk of being attacked call into question the longer-term feasibility of the flows," said Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"This ultimately warrants a sticky risk premium to remain in pricing," McKay told clients in a Thursday note.

articles.title_orig: What Smart People Say About PERM Suspension on Microsoft and Indian Tech
articles.title_zh: What Smart People Say About PERM Suspension on Microsoft and Indian Tech
articles.content_orig:
For foreign workers at some of the biggest employers in tech, there's another twist in an already uncertain system.
The Trump administration’s decision to suspend Microsoft, Adobe, and other named tech companies from the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program has renewed debate over whether stricter skilled-immigration policies protect American workers or hurt American businesses.
On Thursday morning, Vice President JD Vance announced the suspension at a press conference. He singled out Microsoft , saying: "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants."
PERM is not a visa. It is the Labor Department certification employers generally need before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card. Vance said that some companies had abused the system and used foreign workers to undercut Americans.
In a statement on Thursday, Microsoft disputed Vance's accusations, saying most of its H-1B filings were for existing employees rather than new hires.
"Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people," the company wrote.
The action also affects six major IT services companies with deep ties to India’s tech sector: Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, and Capgemini.
Here’s what immigration-policy experts and Indian tech voices are saying:
"Technology companies depend heavily on the 'H-1B-to-green-card' pipeline to retain specialized foreign talent," Hector Chichoni, a partner at the business law firm Greenspoon Marder, told Business Insider.
"With the PERM process effectively frozen, affected companies cannot move employees forward toward permanent residence , making them vulnerable to the loss of critical talent, either to employers not subject to the suspension or through employees returning to their home countries," he added.
Chichoni said the affected IT companies are likely to "vigorously defend themselves" against the allegations the government has made.
The decision also will have a particularly significant impact on Indian tech professionals who are already facing decades-long green card backlogs , Chichoni said.
Hira, a Howard University political science professor and a longtime critic of the H-1B program, called the move against Microsoft “very significant.”
Hira has long argued that employers can use the program in ways that depress pay and disadvantage US workers. He told the Associated Press on Thursday that there are supposed to be protections requiring employers to show that hiring an H-1B worker does not hurt similarly employed Americans.
“That’s never been enforced,” Hira said.
Rand, a former senior advisor at US Citizenship and Immigration Services during the Biden administration, took the opposite view. He called Vance’s announcement “incoherent” in a statement to AP.
Rand’s argument is that the policy could worsen the problem Vance says he wants to solve. H-1B workers are generally tied to their employers for their immigration status. A green card gives workers far more freedom to switch jobs and bargain over pay.
“If the Trump administration were truly concerned that H-1B workers are ‘indentured servants,’ then the last thing they would do is block companies from helping their own H-1B workers get green cards,” Rand told AP.
Pai, an India-based vice president of investments at the country's largest brokerage Zerodha, reacted to what a more restrictive US path to permanent residency could mean for India.
In a statement on X, Pai wrote that the immediate downside could be fewer high-earning Indians in the US, which in turn could mean lower remittances, less soft power, and less angel investments flowing back into Indian startups. He also noted that India receives roughly $125 billion in annual remittances, with the US accounting for about a quarter of that total.
But he also saw a potential upside. If US companies cannot bring talent to America, he wrote, “they probably will bring the work to India.”
US visa uncertainty may also keep more top engineers in India to build domestic companies and AI startups, he added.
Nasscom, India's main tech industry group, said immigration policy and skilled-talent mobility should be treated as separate issues.
"While the decision affects a specific immigration pathway, Nasscom has consistently maintained that immigration and skilled talent mobility are two distinct issues and should not be viewed through the same lens," the group said in a statement to local media
It also said the number of employees moving from H-1B status to permanent residency through PERM is “relatively limited.”

articles.title_orig: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.title_zh: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia.
Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race.
Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir.
The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two.
Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution.
The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually.
Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste.
But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes.
In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions.
“Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added.
Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event.
Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others.
This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead.
Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.”
F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.”
Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.”
Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.
Laura Paddison contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.title_zh: Museum honours two key World War Two RAF stations
articles.content_orig:
A museum has paid tribute to two former RAF stations that played vital roles in Bomber Command operations during World War Two.
The RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum has opened on Lancaster Way Business Park in Ely, Cambridgeshire, to show the contribution RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal made to the Lancaster bombers' offensive.
Grovemere Property bought RAF Witchford from the Ministry of Defence after the war and redeveloped the site.
"It really is just amazing that we are now home to all these wonderful items and can ensure that the experiences and sacrifices of those connected with the two airfields are remembered and understood by future generations," Thomas Brand, from the firm, said.
In 2024 the Brand family, which owns Grovemere Property, decided to create a new free purpose-built museum following the closure of the RAF Witchford Exhibition, which was located in the foyer of an office building on the business park.
The museum is an unmanned facility with the public gaining entrance via a traffic light system taken from an original Lancaster bomber aircraft [John Devine/BBC]
Brand, a joint managing director of Grovemere Property whose grandfather bought the former RAF Witchford airfield, said the origins of the new museum could be traced to an excavation of a Lancaster bomber crash site at nearby Coveney in 1995.
"The project was supported by Grovemere Property, after local historian Barry Aldridge, who spent decades documenting RAF Witchford's history, got in touch," he said.
Aldridge, who died in 2016, had connections to the airfield that stretched back to childhood, when he explored its derelict buildings.
Artefacts recovered during the Coveney dig included a Lancaster engine, which later became a key exhibit in the previous RAF Witchford Exhibition, and is now the centrepiece at the new museum.
One of the exhibition's photographs shows Princess Elizabeth visiting RAF Witchford in 1944 with King George VI and Queen Elizabeth [RAF Witchford and Mepal Museum]
Brand said that many local people had donated items for the museum, which had given him "goosebump" moments.
"Recently a man gave me an old suitcase which contained his late father's RAF uniform, his medals, flight logs, flying helmet and a personal journal that documented his time in the RAF, it was incredible to see," he said.
RAF Witchford and RAF Mepal played key roles in Bomber Command operations, which saw Lancaster bombers fly missions across occupied Europe [John Devine/BBC]
Brand also said he had witnessed some emotional visitors who had found pictures of their loved ones displayed as part of the exhibit.
He did not disclose how much the museum cost to set-up, but said it was now being run as a charity "to help ensure its long-term future".
The striking design of the building incorporates one side of a Lancaster Bomber fuselage which can be viewed from inside [John Devine/BBC]
