Flavio Bolsonaro said he would work with the US and China if he becomes Brazil’s president, after a surprise election performance left him poised to join a wave of conservative leaders pushing Latin America closer to Washington.
Bolsonaro finished ahead of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by about two points in Sunday’s first-round election, a result that sparked a surge in Brazilian assets due to investor views that he is more likely to pursue market-friendly financial policies.
Bolsonaro would take 52 per cent to Lula’s 48 per cent of valid votes, excluding blank and invalid ballots, in the October 25 run-off, a Datafolha poll released on Thursday evening showed. articles.title_orig: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.title_zh: Aspen One begins work on world’s first battery-backed chairlift
articles.content_orig:
Aspen One announced their plans at Wednesday’s annual Afternoon Blend event to make history with the introduction of the world’s first battery-backed chairlift on Snowmass Mountain.
The first phase of the installation happened on Wednesday.
“There are over 4,000 ski lifts in the world,” said Chris Miller, senior vice president of sustainability at Aspen One. “We are doing something for the first time here at Snowmass.”
Following a successful season with the new Elk Camp high-speed six-pack lift at Snowmass, Aspen One is now looking to replace the 1,250 kilowatt diesel generator with a 900 kilowatt battery backup, avoiding approximately 144 tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year going forward.
“We really do set the standard for resort operations in our industry, from a guest experience but also from a sustainability perspective,” Miller said. “Having an impact in the work that we do is super important.”
Every summer, fuel for lifts is pumped out of diesel tanks at the top of Snowmass, with trucks routinely making trips up and down the mountainside for fuel replacement, according to Miller.
“It’s bad from an environmental perspective, and you just don’t want to be moving that stuff up and down the mountains,” he added.
According to him, the new battery backup will be quieter and cleaner than the current generator as well as be charged with nearly 100% clean energy from Holy Cross Energy.
What’s happening in Aspen, in one click.
Sign up for our morning newsletter at AspenTimes.com/newsletter
Part of the challenge of getting the current 92% renewable energy at Holy Cross Energy to 100% is meeting peak demand periods, Miller explained, which requires supplemental non‑renewable generation to meet consumer needs.
Clean energy will back up the lift during the day, and when the lift stops running at 4 p.m., Holy Cross Energy can pull power back into the grid to support local energy demands.
“Aspen One is really at the forefront of helping Holy Cross get to 100% clean energy with the flexibility of these clean storage systems,” said Mike Steiner, key accounts specialist at Holy Cross. “We utilize these batteries to help shave peak demand and manage our renewable energy supply.”
Steiner told The Aspen Times that Holy Cross Energy and Aspen One have aspirations to expand this battery-backed system further, and continue reaching toward cleaner energy and a more sustainable environment.
“We’re going to install this and make sure it’s fully operational and run efficiently,” he said. “We’re working with them closely on a long-term planning approach.”
The project team expects to reach full completion early next month, Miller confirmed in his presentation on Wednesday.
This spooky season, bears don’t need an invitation to trick or treat.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s Plague Scare Revives COVID-Era Anxiety on Chinese Internet
articles.title_zh: Russia’s Plague Scare Revives COVID-Era Anxiety on Chinese Internet
articles.content_orig:
A mysterious death at a Russian anti-plague institute is stirring COVID-era anxiety in China, just five weeks after Chinese and Russian health officials rehearsed a response to an imported plague outbreak.
Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died last week after developing severe pneumonia. Early reports suggested she may have contracted pneumonic plague after breaking a test tube containing plague bacteria, but Russia’s health watchdog said investigators had identified no accidents involving pathogens at the institute and described her illness as “pneumonia of unknown etiology.”
The death prompted authorities to quarantine about 200 people who had been in contact with her . By Thursday, the watchdog said medical observation had ended for all contacts, and nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had found no dangerous pathogens . It also denied reports of a second case.
The World Health Organization, however, says it still does not have the “full picture.”
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the agency has asked Russia for the deceased worker’s laboratory results, an explanation for what prompted the extensive public-health measures, and clarification of reports about another employee with unexplained pneumonia.
The U.S. Embassy in Moscow also issued a health alert , advising its citizens not to travel to Russia and citizens already there to “depart immediately.”
For Chinese netizens, the timing has made the story particularly combustible, reviving uncomfortable memories of the information vacuum and lockdown fears that accompanied the early days of the COVID-19 outbreak.
From August 24 to 27, just over five weeks before Shipilova’s death, China and Russia held a major cross-border infectious disease emergency exercise in Fuyuan, Heilongjiang , on the Russian border.
Chinese readout said the exercise simulated emergencies including “plague imported from abroad and a joint cross-border response,” as well as the discovery of a hypothetical emerging tick-borne “Disease X.”
Sergey Balakhonov, director of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute, was among the Russian officials who attended and spoke at the exercise. Another strand of speculation has focused on He Dahai, Fuyuan’s Communist Party secretary, who also took part in the drill. He has largely disappeared from public view since then, prompting claims that he may have been quarantined .
These coincidences have fueled speculation online. Posts circulating on Weibo, China’s equivalent of X, have invoked memories of China’s three years of Covid controls. Several related topics have surged to the platform’s trending search list, including “ COVID also began as pneumonia of unknown cause” (新冠刚开始也是不明原因肺炎) .
One Weibo user called for China to “maintain strict defense” to avoid “repeating the COVID experience.” Others compared Russia’s conflicting early messaging to the uncertainty surrounding the start of Covid.
More alarmist posts circulating on X and Chinese-language sites have urged residents of Heilongjiang, Jilin and Liaoning to stockpile masks, alcohol, medicine and food , warning that northeastern cities could soon face lockdowns.
A CGSP review of Chinese e-commerce platforms found that many doxycycline listings, an antibiotic used to treat plague, were marked out of stock. Chinese netizens also reported that the drug’s price had risen fivefold in just three days .
So far, Beijing has given little additional information about its communications with Moscow. Asked on Tuesday whether Moscow had contacted China over the suspected pneumonic-plague case, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun replied only that “China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation in the prevention and control of infectious diseases, including plague.”
Public-health experts, however, say the epidemiological evidence so far gives little reason to expect another Covid-like crisis. Pneumonic plague is dangerous and can spread through respiratory droplets, but it is a bacterial disease that antibiotics can treat when detected early.
The scare comes as Russian presidential aide Nikolai Patrushev arrived in China on Thursday for a six-day visit . Patrushev, who also chairs Russia’s Maritime Board, is expected to meet Wang Yi and other Chinese officials. Beijing says their talks will cover bilateral relations and maritime cooperation, but neither side has indicated that the Irkutsk incident will be on the agenda.

articles.title_orig: Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
articles.title_zh: Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
articles.content_orig:
Home → ← News → Preview: ARA Australian Cycling Team ready to battle at UCI Gravel World Championships
The rainbow jerseys are up for grabs in Nannup, Western Australia this weekend, as the UCI Gravel World Championships land on Australian soil for the first time.
A deep roster for the ARA Australian Cycling Team will line up on home turf, ready to go head-to-head with the world’s best and battle for elite men’s and women’s glory.
The Australian squad includes gravel national champion Tiffany Cromwell, who will be racing for the final time before retiring.
With more than 80 per cent of the course unpaved, the stage is set for a gruelling gravel showdown, that will not only test riders' endurance, but also their handling skills on loose sections of gravel.
The elite men will battle across 144km and 3,713 metres of elevation, while the elite women face 125.6km and 3,179 metres of climbing.
Here’s everything you need to know about our athletes chasing the rainbow jerseys, and when and where you can watch.
There have been a number of changes to the Australian squad Australian squad announced earlier , with gravel national champion Cameron Scott and several age-group qualifiers now set to line up in the elite races.
Connor Sens during the 2025 UCI Gravel World Championships. Image: SWPix
Tiffany Cromwell said: "I think I'm pretty content with my decision, and I'm excited to be able to do it on my terms, and here in Australia, like Nannup, it's not Adelaide, but it's as close as I can get to a home race, on the calendar.
“I've been here, I’ve raced SEVEN a couple of times, and it’s such a fantastic event. The team is amazing who put it on. They put so much passion into it.
“The course, it's super demanding, it's super hard. Of course, I've got many good memories here, but I also know, the field that has assembled for the elite women is pretty strong.
“Of course, the dream would be to finish with the rainbows or even just a podium, but also I don't want to put that pressure on myself.
“I want to just be here, be in the moment, enjoy the race, and just give everything that I have mentally, physically left in my body one last time, and just kind of enjoy the last race.”
Australian fans will be able to watch the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships on SBS On Demand . Coverage will begin at 9.45am AWST/12.45pm AEDT on both Saturday and Sunday.
Start lists, detailed schedules, live timing and official results are available at the competition hub .

articles.title_orig: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.title_zh: At least 30 dead in Russian bus strike as Moscow closes in on Ukraine’s ‘fortress belt’
articles.content_orig:
Russian glide bomb hits buses in Ukraine's Kramatorsk, killing at least 30
Kyiv, Ukraine – A Russian glide bomb struck two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian town of Kramatorsk on Thursday morning, killing at least 30 people and wounding 18, regional authorities said.
Ukrainian officials said the attack was deliberate. When dropped from planes on the Russian side of the front line, such bombs can glide to fixed coordinates on the ground, in this case, a street in the town that lies about 20 kilometres (12.4 miles) from the front line.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” regional administration head Vadym Filashkin wrote on Telegram. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill the maximum number of people.”
“Russia consciously disregards all conceivable rules of warfare and norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians,” he wrote.
Filashkin ordered the suspension of the movement of all public transportation in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk as Russia intensifies attacks, paralysing Ukraine’s transport infrastructure, from trains and minibuses to gas stations, bridges, seaports and freight ships.
“This is a new Russian tactic,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “They used to focus on depriving Ukraine of power, on switching off electricity and heating; now their task is also to immobilise the infrastructure, create a transportation collapse.”
“Unfortunately, Russia’s tactic has a certain effect with their strikes on railroads, gas stations,” he said. “They coerce to peace on their conditions.
“They also strike the public psychologically, disrupt the usual lifestyle in general.”
Throughout the war, Russia has denied it targets Ukrainian civilians, a statement that means little to Ukrainians. During the first eight months of 2026, 15,280 civilians were killed or injured, according to the United Nations – a toll that is 55 percent higher than during the same period in 2025.
With no civilian planes in the sky since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion, trains, buses and trucks have become a lifeline for Ukrainian civilians and businesses, as well as for transporting military and humanitarian supplies.
Trains handle almost two-thirds of Ukraine’s freight volumes, including the export of steel slabs, grains and vegetable oils that keep the economy afloat.
At least 521 locomotives have been hit by drones and shelling since 2022, three-fifths this year alone, Ukrzaliznytsia, the state-run railway monopoly, said in late September.
Some locomotives were struck while in motion, and drones have occasionally hit passenger carriages, causing fires, deaths and injuries.
The largest such attack killed five passengers in January in the northeastern Kharkiv region, an act of “terrorism” that was “not militarily justified”, said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Hitting moving trains and buses has become possible because a new generation of Russian drones are no longer the slow, unmanned aircraft that can be jammed electronically or shot down with a machinegun or even an assault rifle.
Jet-powered, with bigger payloads, they are piloted by human operators who use a wireless mesh network, in which each drone serves as a relay node.
“They’re operated manually. The Russians improved their comms,” Andriy Pronin, one of the pioneers of drone warfare in Ukraine, told Al Jazeera.
Occasionally, the signal reaches the drones through a modem on the ground, on a rooftop or even inside somebody’s apartment – switched on by Ukrainians recruited by Russian intelligence, he said.
Locating the modems before attacks is “complicated, but doable”, Pronin said.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, prosecutors and officials, hundreds of recruits, including teenagers, have been offered money via Telegram. They often did not realise the consequences of their actions and have been arrested and convicted.
The video feed and geolocation are often backed by smuggled Ukrainian SIM cards or signals from mobile phone providers in neighbouring, pro-Moscow Belarus, officials believe. These drones can now get almost anywhere in Ukraine, including once-safe western regions.
A train carrying former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson crossed into Poland on September 14, just 30 minutes before a Russian drone struck another passenger train’s locomotive at Yahodyn train station in western Ukraine. Former CIA chief David Petraeus was on a nearby train and reportedly described the attack as “terrifying” and “the act of a truly barbaric leader”.
Ukrainian civilians are equally terrified.
When a daytime Russian drone attack began on September 23, Alyna realised that her workplace was in the most vulnerable place in Kyiv’s central railway station.
She works in a cafeteria located almost in the middle of a massive overpass that stretches above 14 main tracks between the station’s main buildings.
The howling air raid siren and the booms of exploding jet-powered kamikaze drones sent the 24-year-old Kyiv resident scurrying down the stairs and farther on to the subway station.
The drones hit a nearby market, sending black plumes of smoke into the sky and burning to the ground the rotund, modernist building known as the Puck.
“Everything was whistling and rattling above me,” Alyna told Al Jazeera just after another air raid alert ended and passengers began re-entering the station. She withheld her last name for security purposes.
Minutes after the conversation, one more air raid siren forced the passengers out of the railway station, and a drone hit by an interceptor turned into a black cloud in the sky a couple of kilometres east of the building.
The attacks are not limited to trains – Russian drones target petrol stations, buses and minibuses, and seaports, paralysing Ukraine’s exports of grain, vegetable oils and steel.
“You go to a minibus and can hear how [drones] buzz right next to it,” Tetiana Melikhova, a university professor in Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern city with a pre-war population of 720,000, told Al Jazeera.
Her 18-year-old student, Tetiana Bubynets , and two other civilians aged 31 and 48 were killed by an AI-driven drone that was programmed to strike a petrol station on July 6.

articles.title_orig: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
articles.title_zh: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
articles.content_orig:
Chris Murphy says Pentagon blocked him from military base in Qatar and Iran strike on US embassy in Riyadh far worse than public led to believe
Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day.
The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe.
“Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth , was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”.
Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor.
But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon.
In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10.
Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership.
In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region.
“That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.”
Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections.
The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”.
“We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.”

articles.title_orig: Trump calls for Paxton-Talarico debate as Texas Senate race heats up
articles.title_zh: Trump calls for Paxton-Talarico debate as Texas Senate race heats up
articles.content_orig:
James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee.
At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts.
“Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask.
Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.”
Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick.
“James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.”
Talarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person.
“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.”
Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran.
“This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas.
After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28.
During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.”
In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates.
“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote.
The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away.
Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton.
The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton defeated in a bruising Republican primary in May.
A recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed Talarico with a six-point lead over Paxton.
The close nature of the race in a state Trump won by double digits in 2024 is causing anxiety for Republicans, who are flooding the Texas airwaves in the final stretch. GOP ad spending in the state from September to November currently stands at more than $190 million compared to $52 million reserved by Democrats during the same time period.
This article has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: Apple Music Is About To Sound Very Different On Your Apple TV
articles.title_zh: Apple Music Is About To Sound Very Different On Your Apple TV
articles.content_orig:
Apple Music is one of the major music streaming providers, competing with the likes of Spotify, Amazon Music, and Google's YouTube Music. There are differences between the giant companies, which is why some users highlight its ease of use as one of the perks of switching from Spotify to Apple Music . Some listeners also like Apple's lossless audio, which arguably makes it better than YouTube music in terms of sound quality . One popular feature all of them offer is the ability to stream music to your television, playing banger tunes while you complete household chores, get work done, or simply hang out with friends. Still, Apple TV is hoping to stand out with a new feature for its Apple TV 4K 2nd and 3rd-generation devices running tvOS 27.
In September 2026, the tech company said it would transition music streaming to high-resolution lossless audio support for the Apple TV's Apple Music app, providing even more frequencies and data in the stream. Per Apple's support page, lossless audio allows listeners to experience uncompromised tracks spared from any frequency loss. "With an Apple Music subscription, you can turn on lossless audio across all of your devices and hear every preserved detail from the original recording," it says.
Thus, if you own a newer Apple TV 4K model, but haven't yet made the switch to Apple Music, it may be worth a try to experience the sound quality, assuming your speakers are up to the task. Apple said tvOS will only compatible with Apple TV 4K devices released after 2021. Any older Apple TVs will be left behind on this update.
Apple TV's transition to high-res lossless audio for Apple Music came just five years after the service rolled it out for its entire catalog–which contains more than 100 million songs in 2026. Though some listeners may have a hard time telling the difference between hi-res and lossless audio , Mastering Engineer Piper Payne said the former produces an untouched, high quality listening sensation. "The soul and life of the mix is sitting in the extra bits of data that are stored in the lossless file," she said for a June 2021 Apple press release.
When Apple transitioned to high-res lossless, it also added spatial audio with Dolby Atmos support for the service to generate a more immersive atmosphere. "Spatial Audio gives artists the opportunity to create immersive audio experiences for their fans with true multidimensional sound and clarity," the company wrote.
Lossless audio is designed to provide 100% of an original recording despite compression, which certain listeners find more pleasant to the ear. Some reddit users likened its sound quality to that found on CDs and, to others, even vinyl records. "[Lossless audio is] literally CD quality audio," one user wrote. "Like the same sample rate every CD has, the same dumb CDs you were playing in your Chevy Cavalier back in high school."

articles.title_orig: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.title_zh: Canadian author Anne Carson wins literature Nobel for 'bold and inventive' works that blend genres
articles.content_orig:
Anne Carson, the Canadian writer and classicist whose work blends verse, prose and essay with influences from classical myths, has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in literature for her “bold and inventive oeuvre.”
Carson, 76, is an accomplished classicist who has taught at multiple colleges in the US and Canada while also producing works like “The Beauty of the Husband,” “An Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” and “Nox.” Her distinctive essays, prose and poetry, in which the ancient and modern live side-by-side, have garnered her critical acclaim.
Carson’s “playful dialogue with the classical tradition has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Nobel committee said in a statement.
The prize, announced at the Swedish Academy in Stockholm on Thursday, carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor ($1.2 million).
Carson is widely known for hybrid style where she balances multiple ideas, genres and forms. “Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chairman of the Nobel Committee for Literature.
For example, in “Autobiography of Red,” the work that made her name, her long narrative verse is framed by an erudite, enigmatic discussion of Stesichorus, the Greek poet who inspired her. In Stesichorus’ original myth, Heracles – better known by his Latin name of Hercules – kills the winged monster Geryon and steals his red cattle as one of his 12 labors. In Carson’s 1998 retelling, she recasts Geryon as a “tender ‘hero’ devoted to his mother,” who “having earlier been subjected to sexual assaults at the hands of his brother, falls in love with the smug and boorish Heracles,” the Nobel committee said.
Such a complicated form belies the simplicity of much of the language in it. “Somehow Geryon made it to adolescence.// Then he met Herakles and the kingdoms of his life all shifted down a few notches,” Carson writes. “They were two superior eels//at the bottom of the tank and they recognized each other like italics.”
Carson was in Iceland, “listening to the wind,” when she discovered she had won the Nobel Prize, according to Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy.
“She was taken by surprise but very happy – I could hear that in her voice,” Carlberg said.
Much of Carson’s early career was dominated by her work in classics – she studied for her bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees at the University of Toronto and also received a diploma in classics from the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Although she published an essay and her Ph.D. thesis in her thirties, it wasn’t until she was 42 years old that her first book of poems “Short Talks” was published. Three more works followed before “Autobiography of Red” marked her out as a critical favorite.
“The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos,” which charts the breakdown of a marriage between two unnamed characters, came three years later. For that work, Carson became the first female winner of the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize in 2001. She is the 19th woman of the 122 individuals who have won the Nobel Prize for literature.
Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
Carson is notoriously private about her personal life, but her 2010 work “Nox” reflects on the life and death of her estranged brother, Michael. It is not a traditional book, as such, but a “box containing an accordion-fold-out of picture, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” Olsson said.
Carson has also produced several translations of classical texts and ventured into other artforms, collaborating with visual artists, choreographers, opera and theater directors. The transition into various other artistic fields “demonstrates the freedom with which she relates to literary expectations and rule systems, which in turn lies behind the outstanding importance her work since the 1990s has had for the international art and literature scene,” Olsson added.
Last year, the prize went to László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art,” the committee said.
In 2024, South Korean author Han Kang was honored by the committee for her “intense poetic prose that confronts historical traumas and exposes the fragility of human life.”
Literature is the fourth prize to be handed out this week, after achievements in medicine, physics and chemistry. The Nobel Peace Prize is set to be revealed on Friday, followed by the winners in economics on October 12.

articles.content_orig:
The publication “International Trade Outlook for Latin America and the Caribbean 2026” will be presented at a press conference on Thursday, 15 October in Santiago, Chile.
On Thursday, 15 October, the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) will present its annual report International Trade Outlook for Latin America and the Caribbean 2026: The importance of modern services exports and how to promote them. In addition to analyzing the evolution of international trade of economies in the region during the first semester of 2026 and presenting projections of their exports and imports of goods and services for the full year, this ECLAC report also examines the changes being experienced in world and regional trade in the new geopolitical landscape, marked by deep ruptures but also new opportunities for Latin America and the Caribbean.
The document addresses the deep reconfiguration being experienced in world trade, centered on economic security, resilience, and sustainability, and marked by the rapid progress of emerging technologies, a resurgence of productive development policies, and the geographic reorganization of value chains.
The report provides data on the evolution of international trade of goods and services for Latin America and the Caribbean in 2026 and how current geoeconomic and geopolitical transformations are affecting the region. According to the report, in the current landscape marked by uncertainty and geopolitical and geoeconomic tensions, trade has maintained considerable dynamism. Commercial flows of goods from Latin America and the Caribbean have been dynamic throughout 2026, and prospects for the full year are positive.
The second section of the document analyzes the current situation of modern services exports from the region—business, professional, financial, audiovisual, creative, information technology, and research and development services—and argues that there is significant potential to expand these exportations, examining the strategies and instruments used by different countries to drive exportation of modern services in order to recognize good practices, institutional capacities, and lessons learned that can orient policy design and implementation in Latin America and the Caribbean.
This report, prepared each year by the International Trade and Integration Division of ECLAC, will be presented in a hybrid (in-person and virtual) press conference at the Commission’s headquarters in Santiago, Chile at 11:00 a.m. local time (UTC/GMT -3:00), led by the Commission’s Executive Secretary, José Manuel Salazar-Xirinachs.
The media are invited to attend the press conference, which will be held at the ECLAC building (Av. Dag Hammarskjöld 3477, Vitacura, Santiago, Chile, Sala Celso Furtado). The full electronic version of this new edition of ECLAC’s annual report, along with a press release and PDF of the presentation by the Executive Secretary with his main conclusions, will be available at the ECLAC website on Thursday, 15 October, as soon as the press conference has ended.

articles.title_orig: China breakthrough may push sustainable jet fuel gross profit margin past 50%
articles.title_zh: China breakthrough may push sustainable jet fuel gross profit margin past 50%
articles.content_orig:
Biomass-to-jet fuel conversion method could boost production and help meet global aviation industry’s net-zero carbon goals, researchers say
Chinese researchers have developed a catalyst that converts synthesis gas into sustainable jet fuel – an advance that could boost production, help meet net-zero carbon goals and yield a gross profit margin above 50 per cent.
Based on a techno-economic analysis that modelled a planned 100,000-tonnes-per-year jet fuel plant, the researchers estimated they could achieve a gross profit margin of over 50 per cent.
“The excellent pilot test results and the positive techno-economic and life-cycle assessments underscore its strong potential for industrial deployment,” the team said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature Communications in September.

articles.title_orig: US health secretary Kennedy launches new push on vaccine injuries
articles.title_zh: US health secretary Kennedy launches new push on vaccine injuries
articles.content_orig:
Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
The most obvious benefit of having a flu vaccine is to prevent yourself from being infected with the flu. But a flu vaccine also helps keep the disease from spreading to other people. Annual flu vaccines offer significant benefits to those at risk for flu complications, to them an influenza …
WASHINGTON — Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. launched an agencywide effort to study and document any health problems reported after vaccination, the Department of Health and Human Services said on Thursday.
The initiative is the latest step by Kennedy, who spent years questioning vaccine safety and founded an anti-vaccine group before taking office, to reshape federal immunization policy.
The American Academy of Pediatrics says childhood vaccines are studied in placebo-controlled and comparison-group trials and monitored for safety after approval.
The federal Vaccine Injury Table lists 14 compensable injuries across 16 vaccine types under the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, a no-fault system in which claimants file against the government, not vaccine makers. Since 1988, it has awarded about $5 billion across about 12,300 injury and death claims.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks Sept. 1 during an event at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington.
The new moves, which appear to be part of Kennedy's decadeslong efforts to sow skepticism about vaccines, come as he faces legal challenges to his attempts to alter U.S. childhood vaccination schedules and growing concern among public health experts about falling immunization rates, particularly against measles, which has seen a resurgence in the U.S. since last year.
The effort centers on a National Institutes of Health clinic opened Monday to treat and study patients reporting health problems after receiving vaccines, HHS said in a statement.
Other measures include a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposal to reimburse physicians for reporting suspected injuries to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS, a CDC effort to update VAERS and HHS requiring electronic health records to capture vaccine-related adverse events.
Kennedy said U.S. children receive too many vaccines, falsely claiming repeatedly that kids get up to 90 doses before age 18, which was echoed by President Donald Trump. Kennedy long argued that chemicals in vaccines are dangerous, though experts say there is no evidence of harm.
But the bad news is it likely won’t help you out at all. Veuer’s Tony Spitz has the details.
In his first year heading HHS, Kennedy fired all 17 independent expert members of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee and selected new panelists, many of whom shared his anti-vaccine views.
In January, the CDC announced a revamped childhood vaccine schedule that reduced recommended vaccines, dropping universal recommendations for flu, rotavirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis B at birth, some forms of meningitis and respiratory syncytial virus.
A federal court issued a preliminary injunction in March blocking key parts of the proposed changes, finding Kennedy and HHS violated federal law in reshaping the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The injunction prevented ACIP from holding meetings to make recommendations on immunizations often needed for insurance coverage.

articles.title_orig: Station Logs Catch Alaska EAS Test
articles.title_zh: Station Logs Catch Alaska EAS Test
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Several Emergency Alert System participants reported receiving a nationwide test of the EAS on Wednesday. It was intended only for Alaska.
The National Periodic Test (NPT) fired Oct. 7 at 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time with the following message:
“Nationwide Test of the Emergency Alert System. Log Only. The United States Government has issued a Nationwide Test of the Emergency Alert System for all of Alaska beginning at 2:20 p.m. and ending at 2:35 p.m.”
According to an Oct. 8 newsletter from the Alabama Broadcasters Association Engineering Services, the test was conducted by FEMA for Alaska. It was not meant to be forwarded with the “log only” designation.
A similar NPT is scheduled for Puerto Rico on Oct. 15, according to the ABA.
It’s unknown whether the Alaska test was planned specifically in advance of next month’s National Periodic Test, scheduled for Nov. 17 . Radio World reached out to FEMA on Wednesday for further information.
But the test ended up serving as a trial run. And several stations, including facilities in Alabama and Michigan, received the test in their logs because their NPT filters were set to all areas, the ABA reported.
“We have previously reminded stations to select ‘local area’ for all incoming filters,” the ABA wrote.
The ABA emphasized that this setting will not affect state or national alerts, which are issued for all counties.
It also suggested that EAS participants confirm all incoming test areas are set to “local area” in their configuration files. That local area should include every county in a station’s service area.
Harold Price, president of Sage Alert Systems, told the ABA that the Sage ENDEC does not require a user-supplied filter for the NPT, as a 2016 firmware release includes an internal filter.
If a station received and relayed the NPT from Alaska, Price offered this advice:
“Note that your existing EAN filter probably has either no location listed or has ‘all locations’; both forms will match any incoming location in the alert for EAN codes. This was the original workaround for the lack of an all-of-U.S. location code. Now that there is such a code, ‘all locations’ is no longer desired.”

articles.title_orig: Florida officials urge preparation as state braces for first hurricane in two years
articles.title_zh: Florida officials urge preparation as state braces for first hurricane in two years
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias is headed for a Gulf Coast landfall Friday night with life-threatening storm surge, rainfall flooding and high winds. It will then spread its heavy rain and wind inland over the Southeast this weekend.
Preparations to protect life and property from damaging winds and storm surge near the northern Gulf Coast should be finished by tonight.
New this morning: Isaias continues to strengthen and should become a Category 3 major hurricane later this morning.
(MORE: Hurricane Isaias maps tracker | Live updates )
Isaias is centered in the Gulf about 200 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River. The storm is moving to the north-northeast at 15 mph.
It's expected to strengthen more this morning and then will take a more northerly track to landfall.
Set The Weather Company as a 'Preferred Source' to get quicker access to the news you value.
Storm surge warning : Mouth of the Mississippi River to the Suwannee River, Florida. A storm surge watch extends south to Yankeetown, Florida.
Hurricane warning: Along the Gulf Coast from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay/Gulf County line in Florida, and also inland in parts of southwest Alabama and the western Florida Panhandle (shaded in purple on the map below).
(MORE: What you can do today to prepare for Isaias )
Tropical storm warning : Along the Gulf Coast from the Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line south of New Orleans to west of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and east of the Bay/Gulf County line to the Aucilla River, Florida. These warnings also extend to much of inland southern Alabama, parts of southeast Mississippi, the rest of the Florida Panhandle not in hurricane alerts and extreme southwestern Georgia (shaded in red in the map below).
Tropical storm watch: From parts of eastern Mississippi, extending north into central Alabama and parts of western Georgia (shaded in yellow in the map below).
( MORE: What all these tropical terms mean )
Isaias is benefiting from Gulf water temperatures well into the 80s and a moist air mass, both favorable for intensification until early Friday. Additionally, Isaias will pass over some of the warmest waters of the Gulf for several hours during the time of the day more favorable for development. This could boost Isaias to Category 3 status by later this morning.
To be clear: We are not expecting Isaias to make landfall as a major hurricane.
Isaias will experience increasing wind shear as it moves farther north Friday nearing its Gulf Coast landfall.
Wind shear is hostile for both developing tropical systems and hurricanes. You can see the wind shear map below; the colors in darker purple and white indicate strong wind shear.
Therefore, Isaias is likely to lose some wind intensity closer to landfall.
For now, the most likely intensity near landfall is a Category 1 or a Category 2 hurricane. But a slight drop in wind speeds right before landfall will do little to diminish the storm's impacts.
(MORE: What you need to know during hurricane season )
The most significant impacts will be felt along and to the east of the storm's track and its inland remnant.
Isaias is also expected to grow in size near landfall, expanding its footprint of impacts.
The map below shows how much inundation of normally dry ground may occur near the coast from water pushing in from the Gulf as the center of Isaias moves ashore Friday night into early Saturday morning, according to the National Hurricane Center.
These values represent the peak flood levels if the storm surge happens around high tide.
This is a life-threatening storm surge, especially in areas shaded in yellow and orange in the map below.
Damaging winds are most likely in areas covered by hurricane and tropical storm alerts, shown in the graphic near the top of this article, from extreme southeast Louisiana and southeastern Mississippi to central and southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and parts of western Georgia.
Winds of at least 40 mph could arrive as soon as this afternoon and continue at least through Saturday morning near the Gulf Coast.
High winds are also possible Saturday into at least Sunday morning farther inland in the Tennessee Valley and Smoky Mountains.
Downed trees, power lines and power outages that could last for hours or multiple days are possible in these areas. Trees could be toppled easier in ground soaked by heavy rain.
Heavy rain from Isaias will arrive along the Gulf Coast Friday, then will push far inland through the rest of the weekend.
As much as 15 inches of rain could fall locally near the Gulf Coast, especially east of the track of the center where training heavy rainbands may persist the longest. Most other areas near the Gulf Coast are forecast to pick up 4 to 8 inches of rain.
Most of the rest of the Southeast is forecast to pick up 1 to 5 inches of rain.
Locally flash flooding is possible over most of the Southeast, Appalachians and parts of the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic this weekend.
(MORE: What is the 'dirty side' of a hurricane? )
As often is the case with landfalling hurricanes, there is a threat for tornadoes in outer rainbands as the center approaches land Friday, then possibly again Saturday in parts of the Southeast.
Today, conditions will begin to deteriorate along the Gulf Coast.
Anywhere from New Orleans to Tallahassee should see the worst of the rain and winds, but rainfall is also expected in central Florida and even into southeastern Georgia.
Saturday, Isaias will move farther inland and weaken, but its impacts will be far from over.
Heavy rainfall and powerful winds will spread inland across the Southeast. Cities like Jackson, Memphis, Nashville, Atlanta, Wilmington, Charleston, Tallahassee and Orlando could see the worst of the conditions.
Sunday, what is left of Isaias will continue to move north, bringing rainfall to parts of the Great Lakes, mid-Atlantic and even the Northeast.
Rainfall will still be ongoing as far south as Savannah and Nashville but will spread to Charlotte, Virginia Beach, Washington, New York City, Philadelphia and Baltimore. Rain could even fall for Cincinnati and Detroit.
If you're near the Gulf Coast in areas covered by hurricane warnings and/or storm surge warnings, complete your preparations now.
If asked to evacuate by local officials, please consider doing so for your own safety.
If remaining home, be prepared for power outages that could last at least several hours or possibly multiple days.
Avoid flood-prone areas and never drive into flooded stretches of roads.
Impact risk The map below shows the general risk from Isaias and its inland remnant, including from rainfall flooding, winds and storm surge near the coast. This map will update throughout the duration of the storm.
The impact levels on the map mean:
(MORE: Stay prepared this hurricane season )
Isaias ( ees-ah-EE-ahs) is one of the trickier names to pronounce on this year's list. To hear the correct pronunciation, listen here .
Isaias replaced "Ike" on one of the Atlantic name lists after that name was retired following the destructive, deadly 2008 hurricane .
It wasn't used during its first year of eligibility in 2014, since we only reached the eighth name, Hanna, that year.
However, the name was used in 2020 for a storm that eventually tracked up the East Coast with destructive winds.

articles.title_orig: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.title_zh: European industry groups call for urgent EU action on China trade
articles.content_orig:
BRUSSELS, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Forty-four European industry associations urged EU members on Thursday to take immediate action to combat ​what they said were unfair Chinese ‌trade practices threatening EU manufacturing and risking further job losses.
The call from the associations representing sectors including metals, chemicals and automotive parts comes a ‌week ​before EU leaders convene ⁠in Brussels to ⁠discuss how best to tackle a growing trade deficit with China of more than €1 billion ($1.12 billion) a day.
The associations said ​the European Union should more effectively use all instruments available to impose trade ⁠defence measures and ⁠adopt a broader approach to look ​at entire value chains, while avoiding negative ​impacts on close European partners, such as ‌Britain, Norway and Switzerland.
They said the European Commission needed more staff to process complaints more rapidly. They also called for ⁠new tools to deal with state-driven distortions.
EU leaders at the summit are set to discuss Franco-German ⁠proposals for ‌expanded trade defence published ⁠on Monday and European Trade Commissioner Maros ​Sefcovic’s ‌two-day trip to Beijing ending ​on Friday. ⁠Sefcovic is seeking to persuade China to agree to cut exports to the EU in one sector, most likely hybrid vehicles.
(Reporting by Philip Blenkinsop; Editing by ​Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: House Democrats ask Kimberly Guilfoyle for records related to alleged pay-to-play scheme
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: House Democrats ask Kimberly Guilfoyle for records related to alleged pay-to-play scheme
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Guilfoyle faces renewed scrutiny over her conduct as U.S. ambassador to Greece after a Donald Trump donor alleged she offered him access to administration officials in exchange for paying a $100,000 American Express bill. The allegation has prompted calls for an investigation, while her lawyer disputes the messages behind the claim.
Eric Deters, a lawyer and former congressional candidate, made the accusation during a Thursday interview with MS NOW. He said Guilfoyle approached him last year, before her Senate confirmation hearing, and offered him connections to government officials if he covered the outstanding balance. Deters called the arrangement "absolutely" a quid pro quo and said he never owed her money. Deters also called Guilfoyle a "grifter."
Messages Deters shared with The Wall Street Journal reportedly show Guilfoyle promising he would be her "Trump ride or die" if he arranged the payment. In another exchange, she allegedly urged him to stop "papering" their conversations and use Signal instead, warning that written records could jeopardize her ambassadorship.
Jesse Binnall, Guilfoyle's attorney, challenged the messages' authenticity in comments to the Journal. He also maintained that Guilfoyle was owed money for travel and speaking engagements she completed before her nomination. Deters rejected that explanation, saying he did not owe her a balance (via The Guardian ).
Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to address the latest allegations when reporters questioned him in Athens on Wednesday and Thursday. He nevertheless called Guilfoyle "a strong ambassador." Vice President JD Vance also expressed reservations about the alleged arrangement but said he "doesn't know the full details."
The dispute follows earlier reporting by The Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle invited Greek lobbyists to official diplomatic meetings and promoted the business interests of a Greek construction and energy company. Those allegations had already drawn concern from Democratic lawmakers overseeing foreign affairs.

articles.title_orig: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
articles.title_zh: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.
Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.
The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped at 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.
Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".
Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.
Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.
"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.
He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating that grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

articles.title_orig: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
articles.title_zh: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
articles.content_orig:
British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday.
The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain.
Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran.
The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100 km (60 miles) north of London, and raised the alarm.
Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested inside the base.
They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being re-arrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under the National Security Act 2023.
RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command operations, as well as a NATO intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations.
Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) ‌west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran , which denied any involvement.
The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used by US forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford.
“We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement.
Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city.
Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said.
“We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defense minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X.
A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement.
“We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

articles.content_orig:
New initiative aims to strengthen US military capabilities as Washington and Beijing compete for leadership in advanced technology
The Pentagon announced on Thursday a new multimillion-dollar initiative for “maintaining American leadership” in quantum computing capabilities amid accelerating competition between the US and China over the military application of advanced technology.
In a press release, the Office of the Under Secretary of Defence for Research and Engineering, which serves as the US Department of Defence’s chief technology adviser, announced that the new initiative, worth around US$350 million, is aimed at strengthening US leadership in quantum computing capabilities to “support national security”.
Quantum computing dominance is a “critical priority” for the Trump administration, said Emil Michael, undersecretary of defence for research and engineering, citing a June executive order to accelerate the technology’s deployment, commercialisation and domestic manufacturing across the US.
“Maintaining American leadership in this field is essential to preserving our technological edge,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
articles.content_orig:
MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis , died on Wednesday while hospitalized.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal’s lawyer announced her death. Known widely as “Maricarmen,” she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain’s housing affordability crisis.
“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Sánchez said in a post on X. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace.”
Elderly Madrid resident who was forcibly evicted dies at 87
The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain’s Parliament who chanted, “Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!”
Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid.
“A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can’t see it,” she said. “It makes me very sad that she can’t see if anything comes of it, if there is any result from all that she has fought for, as well. That’s what angers me the most, honestly.”
Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health.
Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.
Maricarmen’s lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.
“Maricarmen’s case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people’s health,” Duro said.
She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said in a statement Wednesday. “It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal.”
The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain’s government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.
Protesters camped in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.
Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment.
After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.
“Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn’t asking for anything else,” Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. “She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there’s no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial.”
Maricarmen’s plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain’s unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election.
Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: “I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end.”
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences.
“I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage,” the Popular Party leader wrote. “When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect.”

articles.title_orig: Public Radio Audience Continues "Impressive" Financial Support
articles.title_zh: Public Radio Audience Continues "Impressive" Financial Support
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Headlines
Public radio continues to face steep budget deficits after the loss of federal funding. But the surge in donor support in 2025 has largely carried over into 2026, according to the latest Public Radio Techsurvey from Jacobs Media.
Many in the pubcasting community have wondered if donations might slow down over time.
In conjunction with the Public Media Content Collective, Public Radio Techsurvey 2026 gathered input from 17,000 core public radio listeners using email databases of 49 U.S. stations. Jacobs cautioned that the survey does not represent all public radio listeners and is not stratified to the U.S. population.
Fred Jacobs, president of Jacobs Media, said in an online presentation that stations can stave off the effects of government cuts by using smart fundraising measures.
“Up to 72% strongly agree or agree that as a result of the political climate out there, they’re actually increasing their support to public radio, whether we’re talking generations, gender or format. This is truly a great sign, and I think maybe one of the most important slides in the entire deck,” Jacobs said.
Of the core listeners participating in the survey, four of every 10 say they donate every year, but this year they increased their donations, he said. See below (you can click on these slides to enlarge).
Political conditions continue to have a major impact on core public radio listeners, which is fueling fundraising, he said.
In fact, 39% strongly agree that what’s happening in politics will lead them to increase their support for public radio. The research found that women are more likely to feel that way than men.
“There’s a strong possibility that next year will be pretty solid as well,” Jacobs said.
One in five station listeners in the survey anticipate donating a greater amount next year than usual.
The most effective funding pitch for public radio stations (72%) is government funding cuts and the need for listener support. That’s followed by appeals of making public media available for all and then the need to support independent media in the community.
Current economic pressures were also measured. The Techsurvey shows that the economy is affecting the ability of respondents to give. More than half say it is having a negative impact on their spending.
“One in 10 core public radio listeners say they are being affected in a major way, a negative impact in their life as a result of the economy, and then 43% are saying the economy is having a significant effect, negative impact,” Jacobs said.
The public radio “net promoter” score remained at 70 for the second year in a row. It’s ahead of commercial radio but below Christian music radio results, Jacobs said.
Net promoter scores gauge whether core listeners are likely to recommend a public radio station to others. Public radio’s score has remained fairly steady since 2009, spiking to 75 during the covid pandemic.
“I think you’re definitely looking at reactions to the federal cuts as part of this year. In contrast, commercial radio has an average net promoter score of only 48, so that’s quite a gap there. Christian music radio, on the other hand, actually has a whopping 82,” Jacobs said.
When examining the three prominent formats of public radio –—AAA, classical and news/talk — clearly AAA is the big leader with a net promoter score of 80.
“By the way, that’s no fluke. It has been trending that way over the past several years. News/talk fans are the toughest graders with a score of only a 66,” he said.
Those who like public radio spend the vast majority of their time listening. In fact 40% say it’s all they listen to, Jacobs said. An equal amount say they listen to public radio most of the time. Women are the most likely to say they listen all the time, with millennials and Gen X listening less than boomers and the “greatest generation.”
However the aging of the largest subset of public radio core listeners is a concern. “Demos remain in Medicare territory,” Jacobs said.
The average age of those participating in this research project is 66.5 years old, compared to 65 three years ago. Sixty-five percent of listeners in the survey are 65 or up, according to Jacobs.
“The aging of public radio has been a long-time concern. Stations need to look for content, events and connections to achieve greater relevance with younger fans. Generational common threading is important strategically,” Jacobs said.
The study found that being local can give public stations an edge in their market. Nearly 75% agree that it does. It is the case especially among progressively younger Techsurvey respondents, Jacobs says. Men and women are about even in the findings.
However, only 39% strongly agree that the local public radio station they listen to is “well-connected in the local community.” Meanwhile, 46% want their station to have greater visibility in the community.
In the next part of our series about the Public Radio Techsurvey 2026, we will examine how in-car listening dropped even further as listening habits continue to shift to digital.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says it’s focused on turnaround after report it explored Chipotle merger
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says it’s focused on turnaround after report it explored Chipotle merger
articles.content_orig:
Wall Street was buzzing Thursday about a possible merger that would amount to much more than a hill of beans.
Starbucks said it was focused on its turnaround plan after the Financial Times reported that it explored a potential deal to take over Chipotle Mexican Grill.
“Our team is laser-focused on executing our Back to Starbucks strategy,” Starbucks said in a statement. “We have strong momentum and confidence in our long-term growth potential.”
It added that it typically doesn’t comment on what it described as “rumors and speculation” and said it looks forward to sharing its next earnings results later in October.
The FT reported that Starbucks had hired advisers in recent months to work on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. NBC News hasn’t confirmed the report.
A tie-up between the two companies would mean a massive shake-up in the restaurant industry, which is grappling with consumers’ changing their spending and eating habits.
Before the report emerged, sending shares of Chipotle higher by 6.2%, the company had a total market value of about $39 billion. For comparison, Starbucks’ market value is at more than $105 billion.
Chipotle didn’t reply to a request for comment Thursday afternoon.
A deal would also reunite Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol with the company he led before he jumped to Starbucks in 2024.
Investors appeared worried that a deal could be a distraction for Niccol and his company. Starbucks shares fell as much as 6.6% on Thursday but closed the day only slightly lower.
The company is in the midst of a wide-ranging turnaround plan engineered by Niccol, including a redesign of Starbucks stores, new service standards to speed up customers’ orders, a refreshed menu and a reboot for its rewards program.
Just weeks ago, Niccol touted the plan’s results , saying “tremendous progress” has been made. Shareholders have seen promising returns, too. For the year, Starbucks shares are up almost 11%.
That closely tracks with the S&P 500’s 13% return so far this year. Starbucks has also far outperformed the negative 6.7% return that the S&P 500 Consumer Discretionary sector has recorded this year.
Chipotle shares have sagged by more than 11% this year and more than 20% over the last 12 months.
In July, the company’s latest earnings results beat expectations, but that followed a period of slow traffic and price hikes. Those results also came alongside soaring gas prices for consumers.
“We’re seeing encouraging progress because we’re focused on the right growth drivers,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said in a statement in July . Like Starbucks, Chipotle has also revamped its rewards program and made tweaks to its menu to lure customers back.
Chipotle has also started expanding outside the U.S., with plans to open stores in Mexico, South Korea and Saudi Arabia.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
